meta.title: Ordered growth zones for a 3D timelapse of London, c.100 BCE - 2025

field_semantics.year_start: Year building begins in this zone.
field_semantics.year_end: Year the zone is fully built out to the stated density; the polygon traces the built-up extent AT year_end.
field_semantics.kit: Which procedural building kit to instance: celtic, roman, saxon, medieval, tudor, georgian, victorian, interwar, postwar, modern, estate, tower.
field_semantics.density: Fraction of 10 m cells inside the polygon that should carry a building at year_end (0-1). This is the single most important field for realism: medieval and Victorian inner zones run 0.8-0.95, Georgian villa fringes and interwar semis 0.25-0.75, Roman contraction 0.2, envelope zones 0.15-0.6.
field_semantics.area_km2: Computed planar area of the polygon (equirectangular projection at the polygon's mean latitude). Zones overlap heavily by design - the engine should UNION them in order, not sum them.
field_semantics.abandoned: If true this is a NEGATIVE zone: clear/ruin every cell inside it between year_start and year_end. Four exist: Roman abandonment 410-450, Lundenwic abandonment 850-900, Black Death stagnation (see z020 notes), Docklands dereliction 1967-81.
field_semantics.constraint: If true this is a no-build constraint (the Metropolitan Green Belt), not a growth zone.

meta.ordering: Zones are sorted by year_start then year_end. Rasterise in this order; a later zone overwrites an earlier one's kit but must NOT overwrite an earlier birth year for a cell that is already built (except where 'abandoned' is set, or where an events.json event destroys it).
companion_files: events.json (destruction and rebuild events with polygons)
growth_summary.md (narrative and the year -> area table)

keys.estates: 60 named council/public housing clusters with lon/lat/radius_m
keys.towers: 18 tall-building clusters with lon/lat/radius_m and heights
keys.voids: 35 permanent open spaces and water bodies that must never be built on

meta.accuracy_note: Polygons are hand-drawn generalisations of historic map evidence (Agas c.1561, Braun and Hogenberg 1572, Faithorne and Newcourt 1658, Morgan 1682, Rocque 1746, Horwood 1799, Greenwood 1827, Stanford 1862, Booth 1889, Bacon 1900, OS 1914 and 1935, Abercrombie 1944, ONS built-up area 2011). Expect 100-300 m of positional error on a pre-1700 boundary and 300-800 m on a suburban edge; they are good enough to drive a 3-minute timelapse and are NOT survey data. Dates are firm where a statute, a station opening, a lease or a completion is recorded, and approximate (stated as such in the notes) elsewhere.

zones.name: Late Iron Age farmsteads on the Thames terrace (future City hills)
zones.notes: There was NO oppidum or town on the Londinium site before AD 43. Excavation on Ludgate Hill and Cornhill has produced only residual Late Iron Age pottery, a few ditches and a possible farmstead, plus a ford/ferry crossing near Westminster. Render this zone at ~3 percent cell occupancy (a handful of roundhouse groups) so the site reads as inhabited countryside, not a town. Genuine Late Iron Age sites in the wider frame (Uphall Camp Ilford, Caesar's Camp Wimbledon, Heathrow, Woolwich Power Station) are carried in villages.json, not here.
sources: Museum of London / MOLA: Londinium was a de-novo Roman foundation

zones.name: Londinium founded - first town on Cornhill and the bridgehead
zones.notes: Dendrochronology from a Roman drain on Fenchurch Street gives a felling date of AD 47, the conventional foundation date. The first town was a planned strip-building settlement on the east (Cornhill) hill either side of the main road from the bridge (Fish Street Hill) and along the Cheapside-Lombard Street axis, with the Walbrook stream as its western edge. About 25-40 ha occupied by AD 60, timber and clay-and-daub, thatch and tile. Tacitus: 'copia negotiatorum et commeatuum maxime celebre' - crowded with traders.

zones.name: Roman Southwark bridgehead suburb
zones.notes: Built on two low sand and gravel eyots in the Thames floodplain (the 'north island' at the bridge foot, the 'south island' near modern Borough station), linked by causeway. Strip buildings along the approach road (modern Borough High Street), a mansio, temples, cemeteries to the south along Watling Street. About 15-20 ha. Occupation thinned sharply after c.AD 200 and was largely gone by 400.
sources: Museum of London Archaeology, Roman Southwark

zones.name: Flavian-Hadrianic Londinium at its greatest extent
zones.notes: Rebuilt after Boudica and expanded fast: the second (great) forum-basilica c.AD 90-120 at Gracechurch Street (the largest north of the Alps), the Cripplegate fort c.AD 120 (-0.0955,51.5178), the amphitheatre c.AD 70 rebuilt in stone c.120 under Guildhall Yard (-0.0925,51.5157), public baths at Huggin Hill and Cheapside, and a 1 km timber quayfront. Peak occupied area c.130-140 ha, population 30,000-60,000. Occupation spread west of the Walbrook to the Fleet and north beyond Cheapside. The 'Hadrianic fire' c.AD 125 burned a large part of the town; treat as partial, not total.
sources: Perring, London in the Roman World (2022)

zones.name: The walled city of Londinium (landward wall c.190-225, riverside wall c.270)
zones.notes: The canonical polygon for the walled City - reuse it for every later 'inside the walls' zone. 2.0 miles / 3.2 km of circuit, 6 m high, 2.0-2.6 m thick, enclosing about 330 acres = 133 ha = 1.33 km2, the largest walled area in Roman Britain. Gates (use these for suburb ribbons): Ludgate -0.1032/51.5141, Newgate -0.1013/51.5157, Aldersgate -0.0975/51.5172, Cripplegate -0.0938/51.5183, Moorgate (medieval, 1415) -0.0888/51.5178, Bishopsgate -0.0805/51.5165, Aldgate -0.0760/51.5142. The riverside wall was added c.AD 270. Note that density FALLS after c.160: large parts of the intramural area reverted to 'dark earth' garden and dumping ground even while the wall stood.
sources: English Heritage: History of London Wall

zones.name: Late Roman contraction - dark earth inside the walls
zones.notes: From the later 2nd century onward the built-up fraction inside the walls collapsed. Excavations across the City find a thick homogeneous 'dark earth' horizon over 2nd-century buildings, interpreted as cultivation, dumping and stock-keeping within a still-walled but half-empty town. Population fell to perhaps 10,000-20,000 by 300 and a few thousand by 400. For the timelapse: DELETE cells rather than add them across 200-400, keeping a thin ribbon along the main streets and the public buildings (forum demolished c.300, but the wall, the Tower-Hill riverside bastions of c.350-400 and the Cripplegate fort survive).
sources: Perring, London in the Roman World

zones.name: Sub-Roman abandonment of the walled city
zones.notes: ABANDONMENT ZONE - set every cell inside this polygon to 'ruin' between 410 and 450. Coin supply to Britain stops c.402-411; there is no securely dated 5th-century urban occupation in the walled City. Between roughly 450 and 600 the walled area was ruins and scrub, with only St Paul's (604) reoccupying it. This is the single most dramatic beat available in the whole 2000-year sequence: a walled city that empties completely and stays empty for 150 years.

zones.name: Lundenwic - the Middle Saxon trading town on the Strand
zones.notes: Bede's 'Lundenwic ... an emporium of many peoples coming by land and sea' (c.731). Excavations under the Royal Opera House, Jubilee Hall, the National Portrait Gallery and Maiden Lane found metalled lanes, sunken-featured and post-built halls, and Ipswich and Rhenish pottery. Peak extent c.750-800 was 55-60 ha, population maybe 5,000-10,000, running along the north side of the Strand from about the National Gallery east to Aldwych and north to Shorts Gardens/Long Acre. The Saxon foreshore was roughly on the line of the Strand itself; the Embankment did not exist. Sacked by Vikings 842 and 851, decaying from c.830.
sources: London Museum: Lundenwic, the other medieval London
Layers of London: Excavation and Mitigation in Lundenwic

zones.name: Lundenwic abandoned - 'Ealdwic', the old settlement
zones.notes: ABANDONMENT ZONE. After the Viking attacks of 842/851 and Alfred's refoundation inside the walls in 886, the Strand settlement was given up and reverted to fields and vineyards for 300 years. Its name survives as Aldwych (Ealdwic, 'old settlement'). Clear these cells over 850-900 and do not re-add them until the medieval Strand ribbon (z019) creeps back from about 1200.

zones.name: Alfred's Lundenburg - reoccupation of the walled city
zones.notes: Alfred 'restored' London in 886 and put it in Ealdorman Aethelred's charge. Reoccupation was concentrated in the WESTERN half of the walled area: a new grid of streets between Cheapside and the river (Bread Street, Milk Street, Friday Street - the '-street' names are Saxon), the two new hythes at Queenhithe (Aethelredshythe, charter of 889, -0.0952/51.5110) and Billingsgate (-0.0830/51.5090). The eastern third round Aldgate and the Tower stayed largely empty until the 11th century. The Burghal Hidage burh 'Suthringa geweorche' at Southwark was established in the same generation, c.915.

zones.name: Late Saxon London fills the walls
zones.notes: By 1000 London was the largest town in England, c.15,000-20,000 people, with more than 100 parish churches inside the walls by 1100 - the highest parish-church density in Europe. The rebuilt timber London Bridge (attested 1016, on the modern-day line -0.0882/51.5085) and the growing waterfront let the town fill east to the Tower site. Density 0.7 with sunken-floored cellars and two-storey timber houses; the moor north of the wall (Moorfields) stayed marsh.

zones.name: Westminster - abbey, palace and the King Street village
zones.notes: Edward the Confessor rebuilt the abbey on Thorney Island 1042-1065 (consecrated 28 Dec 1065; Westminster Abbey 51.4993/-0.1273) and moved the royal residence there; William Rufus added Westminster Hall 1097-99 (51.4995/-0.1250). This is a SECOND, physically separate urban nucleus 2.2 km west of the City along the river, and it stays separate - joined to the City only by the Strand ribbon - until the Tudor period. By 1200 it held the abbey precinct, the palace, King Street (the modern Whitehall/Parliament Street line) and a service village of a few hundred people.
sources: Wikipedia: Westminster Abbey; Palace of Westminster
Survey of London vols X, XIII

zones.name: The medieval City fills the walls (Norman to c.1300)
zones.notes: The walled city becomes almost solidly built - jettied timber houses of three and four storeys, 110+ parish churches, the friaries (Blackfriars 1276 -0.1035/51.5122, Greyfriars 1225 -0.0993/51.5162, Austin Friars 1260 -0.0855/51.5155), Guildhall from 1128 rebuilt 1411 (-0.0917/51.5158), Old St Paul's rebuilt from 1087 (-0.0984/51.5138, spire 149 m from 1314), and the Tower of London from 1078 (-0.0759/51.5081) which is OUTSIDE the SE corner of the wall on reclaimed ground. The river frontage advanced c.100 m south of the Roman line by 1300 through successive revetments. Note the waterfront polygon edge here is slightly south of z005. Population c.1300 was 80,000-100,000 in city plus suburbs.
sources: British History Online: Survey of London; A Dictionary of London

zones.name: Medieval Southwark - Long Southwark and Bankside
zones.notes: 'Long Southwark' ran about 1.2 km south from the bridge foot along Borough High Street to St George the Martyr (-0.0930/51.5008), lined with the great galleried inns (Tabard 1307, George, White Hart) because the City gates shut at night. Southwark Cathedral (St Mary Overie priory, 1106) at -0.0880/51.5060; Winchester Palace 1144 at -0.0912/51.5070; the Clink liberty, the stews and bear-gardens on Bankside westward to about -0.0990. Southwark was the City's 26th ward from 1550 but stayed physically a separate ribbon until the 17th century.
sources: British History Online: Survey of London vol 22 (Bankside)

zones.name: Extramural suburb: Smithfield, Charterhouse and Clerkenwell
zones.notes: Outside Aldersgate and Newgate: St Bartholomew's priory and hospital, founded 1123 (-0.0999/51.5188); Smithfield, the horse and cattle market and tournament ground, and site of executions (-0.1010/51.5192); the Charterhouse, 1371, on the 1349 plague burial ground (-0.0994/51.5205); St John's Clerkenwell, the Hospitallers' English priory from c.1144 (-0.1032/51.5216) and St Mary's nunnery c.1145 (-0.1058/51.5222). This zone was monastic precinct and market, not dense housing, until the Dissolution - hold density at 0.4 until 1540 then let z022 take it.
sources: British History Online: Survey of London vol 46; VCH Middlesex

zones.name: Extramural suburb: Fleet Street, Whitefriars and the Temple
zones.notes: The first suburb outside Ludgate, across the Fleet river (Fleet Bridge -0.1046/51.5140). Ribbon development along Fleet Street to Temple Bar (-0.1116/51.5135), with the Temple (Templars from 1161, Inns of Court from c.1320) on the river side at -0.1118/51.5125, Whitefriars 1253, and the bishops' inns. Only 150-250 m deep either side of the street; behind it were gardens.
sources: British History Online: A Dictionary of London (Harben)

zones.name: Extramural suburb: Holborn and the Inns of Chancery
zones.notes: From Newgate down Snow Hill, over Holborn Bridge across the Fleet, and up High Holborn past Ely Place (bishops of Ely, 1290, -0.1076/51.5182), Furnival's Inn, Staple Inn (1585 front survives, -0.1103/51.5177), Gray's Inn (from 1370, -0.1113/51.5192) and Lincoln's Inn (from 1422, -0.1140/51.5157). The ribbon ended at St Giles-in-the-Fields (-0.1272/51.5145), which was a genuinely separate village with a leper hospital of 1101 until the 17th century.
sources: British History Online: Survey of London vol 5 (St Giles-in-the-Fields)
Wikipedia: High Holborn; Inns of Chancery

zones.name: Extramural suburbs: Bishopsgate Without to Shoreditch, and Aldgate to Whitechapel
zones.notes: Two ribbons treated as one zone because they meet at the NE corner of the wall. NORTH: Bishopsgate Street Without past St Botolph's, the priory and hospital of St Mary Spital (1197, -0.0770/51.5185, which gave Spitalfields its name), Norton Folgate, up to St Leonard's Shoreditch (-0.0778/51.5266). EAST: Aldgate High Street, the Minories (nunnery of St Clare 1293), and Whitechapel Road to the chapel of St Mary Matfelon (c.1250, -0.0645/51.5163). Both were ribbons perhaps 120-200 m deep with open fields behind (Spitalfields, Goodman's Fields, Mile End waste) into the 17th century.
sources: British History Online: Survey of London vol 27 (Spitalfields); Stow, Survey of London 1598

zones.name: The Strand ribbon - City to Westminster
zones.notes: The single most important pre-modern growth axis: a ribbon of great riverside houses linking the two nuclei. On the SOUTH (river) side, the bishops' and magnates' inns each with garden and water-gate - the Savoy 1263 (-0.1195/51.5108), Durham House, York Place (from 1240, seized 1529 and rebuilt as Whitehall Palace), Somerset House 1547 (-0.1170/51.5110); on the NORTH side small houses and the villages of St Clement Danes (-0.1130/51.5133) and St Mary-le-Strand. Charing Cross, the last Eleanor Cross of 1291, at -0.1278/51.5074. Depth only 100-200 m; behind it Covent Garden was still the abbey's convent garden and the fields of St Martin.
sources: British History Online: Survey of London vols 16, 18 (Strand)

zones.name: Medieval peak c.1300 and the Black Death contraction
zones.notes: NEGATIVE-GROWTH ZONE. London's medieval population peaked at c.80,000-100,000 around 1300, then the Great Famine 1315-17 and the Black Death of 1348-49 (which killed 40-60 percent) cut it to c.40,000. It did not regain its 1300 level until the 1540s. Physically the city did not shrink much - the plots stayed but tenements decayed, gardens spread inside the walls, and the suburbs stopped growing for 150 years. For the timelapse: freeze all growth 1350-1500 and knock density down by about 20 percent inside the walls and by more in the suburbs, then let Tudor growth (z021+) refill.
sources: Wikipedia: Black Death in England; Demography of London
Barron, London in the Later Middle Ages

zones.name: Tudor Westminster - Whitehall, St James's and the court quarter
zones.notes: Henry VIII seized York Place from Wolsey in 1529 and turned it into Whitehall Palace (-0.1258/51.5045), built St James's Palace 1531-36 (-0.1385/51.5045) and enclosed St James's Park and Hyde Park as hunting grounds. Westminster grew from a village into the seat of government: the law courts fixed in Westminster Hall, Parliament in St Stephen's Chapel from 1548. IMPORTANT: St James's Park (-0.1330/51.5025, ~23 ha) and Green Park lie inside this polygon and must be punched out as voids - see the 'voids' key. Real built cells are the King Street/Whitehall ribbon, Tothill Street, Petty France and the abbey precinct.
sources: Survey of London vols 10, 13, 14 (St Margaret Westminster, Whitehall)
Wikipedia: Whitehall Palace; St James's Palace

zones.name: Tudor Clerkenwell, Smithfield and the Dissolution precincts
zones.notes: The Dissolution of 1536-40 handed a ring of monastic precincts on the City's northern fringe to speculators, and they were the first big private redevelopment in London's history. St John's Clerkenwell, St Mary's nunnery, the Charterhouse (a mansion by 1545), Blackfriars and Greyfriars all filled with tenements and small industry (brewing, clockmaking, distilling). By Stow's Survey of 1598 Clerkenwell and St John Street were continuously built from Smithfield to the Clerkenwell green. This is the earliest zone where London grows by conversion rather than by conquest of fields.
sources: British History Online: Survey of London vol 46 (South and East Clerkenwell)

zones.name: Tudor Bankside and the Southwark liberties
zones.notes: Outside the City's jurisdiction, so the liberties of the Clink and Paris Garden took the trades London would not house: the stews, the bear- and bull-baiting rings, and from 1587 the playhouses - the Rose 1587 (-0.0947/51.5078), the Swan 1595 (-0.0995/51.5070), the Globe 1599 (-0.0959/51.5069), the Hope 1614. Behind the riverside strip, Bankside and Bermondsey Street thickened, and the Borough remained the great inn quarter. On the Agas map (c.1561) the built strip is barely 150 m deep; by Norden 1600 it is 300 m.
sources: British History Online: Survey of London vol 22 (Bankside)

zones.name: Tudor riverside hamlets - St Katharine's, Wapping, Shadwell, Ratcliff, Limehouse
zones.notes: A thin maritime ribbon along the north bank, one or two houses deep, from St Katharine's by the Tower through Wapping (the 'Wapping Wall' built on drained marsh from the 1540s), Shadwell, Ratcliff (the great Elizabethan shipping hamlet, where Frobisher and Willoughby sailed from) and Limehouse (limekilns, ropewalks, shipyards). Behind it, until the 18th century, lay open marsh and market garden. Deptford (1513) and Woolwich (1512) royal dockyards on the south bank are separate settlements - see villages.json.
sources: British History Online: Survey of London vols 27, 43-44 (Poplar, Blackwall and the Isle of Dogs)

zones.name: Tudor East End - Spitalfields, Whitechapel, Goodman's Fields
zones.notes: Stow in 1598 complained bitterly that the fields east of the Tower and along Whitechapel had been 'pestered with cottages' - the first documented working-class suburban sprawl in England. Goodman's Fields (-0.0700/51.5140), East Smithfield, Petticoat Lane and the Old Artillery Ground filled with cheap two-storey timber cottages housing sailors, weavers, brewers and immigrants. Repeated royal proclamations against new building (1580, 1593, 1602, 1607, 1625) were ignored. Density stays modest because behind the ribbons there were still tenter-grounds and market gardens.
sources: British History Online: Survey of London vol 27 (Spitalfields and Mile End New Town)

zones.name: Tudor ribbon infill - Holborn, St Giles, Long Acre, Drury Lane
zones.notes: The two ribbons - Holborn on the north and the Strand on the south - began to be joined by building along Drury Lane, Long Acre and Chancery Lane, closing the gap between the City suburbs and the still-separate village of St Giles-in-the-Fields (-0.1272/51.5145). By 1600 you could walk from Newgate to Charing Cross without leaving houses, but the block between them was still fields (Covent Garden, Lincoln's Inn Fields, Leicester Fields). This zone is the frame; the Stuart squares (z028-z032) fill the interior.

zones.name: Tudor Shoreditch, Hoxton and Old Street
zones.notes: England's first purpose-built playhouses stood here, outside the City's control: The Theatre 1576 (-0.0790/51.5262) and the Curtain 1577 (-0.0787/51.5250), both in Shoreditch. Around them, ribbon cottages along Shoreditch High Street, Old Street and Hoxton Street with tenter-grounds, gardens and Finsbury Fields (the archery ground, still open in 1600) behind. Moorfields immediately south was drained and laid out as London's first public park in 1607 - punch it out as a void until c.1810.
sources: Wikipedia: The Theatre; Curtain Theatre; Moorfields

zones.name: Stuart riverside east - Wapping, Shadwell, Ratcliff, Limehouse, Poplar
zones.notes: The fastest-growing part of 17th-century London by population. Shadwell went from a hamlet to a parish of 8,000 between 1650 and 1680; Wapping, Ratcliff, Limehouse and Poplar (with the East India Company's Blackwall yard from 1614 and almshouses of 1628) formed a continuous 4 km maritime strip by 1700, deepening from one street to five or six. Trades: shipbuilding, ropewalks, biscuit-baking, brewing, lime, tar. Population of the riverside hamlets c.1700 was perhaps 60,000-80,000, comparable to the whole City.
sources: Survey of London vols 43-44 (Poplar, Blackwall and Isle of Dogs)

zones.name: Stuart Southwark, Bermondsey and Rotherhithe
zones.notes: The south bank thickened into a continuous industrial waterfront from Lambeth Marsh east to Rotherhithe: tanneries and leather at Bermondsey (-0.0810/51.4980, the Leather Market and Long Lane), breweries at Southwark (the Anchor), timber yards, glassworks, and from 1700 the Howland Great Wet Dock at Rotherhithe (1696-99, -0.0490/51.5030), England's first commercial wet dock. Still only 300-600 m deep from the river: everything south of the modern New Kent Road was market garden and marsh until after the new bridges of 1750 and 1769.
sources: Survey of London vol 25 (St George the Martyr Southwark); vol 22 (Bankside)
Wikipedia: Bermondsey; Rotherhithe; Howland Great Wet Dock

zones.name: Covent Garden piazza - the first London square
zones.notes: Laid out 1631-37 for the 4th Earl of Bedford by Inigo Jones on the former convent garden of Westminster Abbey: an Italian piazza with arcaded terraces on the north and east, St Paul's Covent Garden church on the west (-0.1225/51.5119, built 1631-33), Bedford House and garden on the south. Licensed by Charles I for a fee of 2,000 pounds against the standing ban on new building. It set the template - landowner's estate, formal square, standardised terraced houses, uniform elevation, ground leases - for the next 250 years of London growth. Fruit and vegetable market from 1654.

zones.name: Lincoln's Inn Fields, Great Queen Street and Holborn squares
zones.notes: Great Queen Street (-0.1215/51.5155) was built c.1629-40 as London's first uniform street of brick houses with a giant order; Lincoln's Inn Fields (-0.1174/51.5155, London's largest square at 2.8 ha) was laid out from 1638 by the speculator William Newton over the lawyers' protests, with Lindsey House c.1640 attributed to Inigo Jones. Red Lion Square followed 1684 (-0.1180/51.5188). Note the square itself is a void: only the perimeter is built.
sources: Survey of London vol 3 (St Giles-in-the-Fields part 1: Lincoln's Inn Fields)
Wikipedia: Lincoln's Inn Fields; Great Queen Street

zones.name: Bloomsbury and Seven Dials - the northern Stuart squares
zones.notes: Bloomsbury (Southampton) Square, 1661, was the first London space actually called a square (-0.1226/51.5195); the 4th Earl of Southampton built Southampton House on its north side with a market and service streets behind, the model for the Georgian estate. Seven Dials followed 1693 (-0.1268/51.5142), Thomas Neale's seven-street star, built cheap and slum by 1750. Beyond, the Lamb's Conduit Fields and the Foundling estate stayed open until the 1790s.
sources: Survey of London vol 5 (St Giles-in-the-Fields part 2)

zones.name: Stuart northern fringe - Clerkenwell, Islington and Hoxton ribbons
zones.notes: Ribbon growth along the two great north roads out of the City - St John Street / Islington High Street to the Angel (-0.1058/51.5330) and Kingsland Road through Hoxton - plus the spa and pleasure-garden belt (Sadler's Wells 1683 -0.1063/51.5292, New River Head 1613 -0.1085/51.5288, Islington Spa 1685). Density is low: this is a scatter of inns, spas, market gardens and terraces along roads with fields between. The New River (1609-13) and its reservoirs must be treated as linear voids.
sources: Survey of London vol 47 (Northern Clerkenwell and Pentonville)

zones.name: St James's - the West End court suburb
zones.notes: Henry Jermyn, Earl of St Albans, obtained the freehold of St James's Fields in 1665 and laid out St James's Square (-0.1355/51.5074) with Jermyn Street, King Street, Duke Street and Charles Street, aiming explicitly at courtiers who wanted to live near Whitehall and St James's Palace. Pall Mall and Piccadilly (Clarendon House 1664, Burlington House 1665, Berkeley House 1665) form the northern edge. This zone establishes the West End as the aristocratic quarter and the fundamental east-poor/west-rich polarity of London, which is driven by the prevailing south-westerly wind carrying City smoke eastwards.
sources: Survey of London vols 29-30 (St James Westminster)
Wikipedia: St James's Square; Henry Jermyn, 1st Earl of St Albans

zones.name: The Great Fire zone rebuilt in brick, 1667-1680
zones.notes: The same polygon as the Great Fire event in events.json - use it twice: destroy in 1666, re-lay in brick 1667-1680. The Rebuilding of London Act 1667 mandated brick or stone, banned jetties, fixed four standard house types by street class, widened the main streets and set up the Fire Court to settle landlord-tenant disputes fast. About 9,000 of the 13,200 lost houses were rebuilt within 7 years, on the OLD street lines (Wren's and Evelyn's grand plans were dropped) - so the medieval plan survives inside a Georgian skin. 51 of 87 lost churches rebuilt by Wren's office 1670-1700; new St Paul's 1675-1710 (-0.0984/51.5138); the Monument 1671-77 (-0.0860/51.5102). Traditional figure for the burnt area is 436 acres (1.76 km2 - 373 acres inside the walls and 63 outside); the measured polygon here is about 1.45 km2 because the acre figures use the larger 'City within the walls' ward area including reclaimed waterfront.
sources: Wikipedia: Great Fire of London; Rebuilding of London Act 1666

zones.name: Soho, Golden Square and Leicester Fields
zones.notes: The last big field between the West End and Holborn. Leicester Square from 1670 (-0.1300/51.5103, around Leicester House of 1635), Soho Square 1681 (-0.1320/51.5150, originally King Square), Gerrard Street, Old Compton Street, Golden Square 1670s-1690s (-0.1372/51.5112). Built quickly and cheaply by Richard Frith and others, and immediately colonised by Huguenot refugees after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685, which is why Soho was multi-ethnic from its first decade.
sources: Survey of London vols 33-34 (St Anne Soho)

zones.name: Spitalfields, Bethnal Green edge and Mile End New Town
zones.notes: The Old Artillery Ground was built over from 1682 and Spital Square/Elder Street/Fournier Street from the 1680s-1720s, filling with Huguenot master weavers after 1685: tall brick houses with wide top-floor weaving lofts (Fournier Street -0.0722/51.5192, still standing). Christ Church Spitalfields, Hawksmoor, 1714-29 (-0.0748/51.5195). Mile End New Town and the western edge of Bethnal Green followed to c.1720. By 1700 this was the densest and poorest quarter of London after the riverside.
sources: Survey of London vol 27 (Spitalfields and Mile End New Town)

zones.name: Mayfair - the Grosvenor, Berkeley and Burlington estates
zones.notes: The classic aristocratic Georgian estate development, built west of the built-up edge onto open fields under 99-year building leases. Sequence: Hanover Square 1713-17 (-0.1430/51.5140); Grosvenor Square 1721-31 (-0.1508/51.5124, 2.4 ha, the Grosvenor family's 100-acre Mayfair estate); Berkeley Square 1738-47 (-0.1465/51.5100); Curzon Street, Shepherd Market (1735 on the site of the May Fair itself, -0.1470/51.5065). Complete by about 1770. Bounded by Oxford Street (north), Park Lane and Hyde Park (west), Piccadilly (south), Regent Street (east, cut later in 1814-25). Uniform brown-brick terraces, 3-5 storeys, iron railings and area steps, mews behind - the single most reusable building kit in the whole model.
sources: Survey of London vols 39-40 (The Grosvenor Estate in Mayfair)

zones.name: Marylebone - the Cavendish-Harley and Portman estates
zones.notes: Built north from Oxford Street to the New Road in three estates. Cavendish Square from 1717 (-0.1454/51.5162, Harley/Cavendish, stalled by the 1720 South Sea Bubble and only finished in the 1760s); the Portman estate with Portman Square 1764-84 (-0.1573/51.5162) and Manchester Square 1776-88 (-0.1521/51.5172); Portland Place 1773-80 by the Adam brothers (-0.1448/51.5205), at 38 m the widest street in London. The New Road (built 1756, now Marylebone Road / Euston Road / Pentonville Road, along 51.5230-51.5300) was the agreed northern limit of building and held that line until the 1790s - a hard, dateable edge that reads beautifully in a timelapse.
sources: Wikipedia: Marylebone; Portman Estate; New Road, London

zones.name: Bethnal Green, Mile End, Stepney and the weaving East End
zones.notes: The Spitalfields silk industry spilled east into Bethnal Green from the 1740s: two-storey weavers' cottages with long first-floor windows, built cheaply on 'building leases' over former brickfields and market gardens. When Spitalfields silk collapsed after the 1826 free-trade treaty the district became the deepest poverty in London - Bethnal Green's population rose from 22,300 in 1801 to 74,100 in 1841 with almost no drainage. Mile End Old Town and Stepney Green filled along the Whitechapel-Bow road (-0.0400/51.5230). The Old Nichol rookery (-0.0745/51.5250) developed here and was cleared for the Boundary Estate in 1890-1900.
sources: Survey of London vol 27; VCH Middlesex vol 11 (Stepney, Bethnal Green)

zones.name: Bloomsbury and Fitzrovia - the Bedford and Foundling estates
zones.notes: The most complete surviving Georgian estate landscape in London, built by the Dukes of Bedford and the Foundling Hospital. Bedford Square 1775-83 (-0.1300/51.5192, the only wholly intact Georgian square in Bloomsbury); Russell Square 1800-04 (-0.1250/51.5210, laid out by Humphry Repton for James Burton); Tavistock Square 1806; the Foundling/Brunswick estate 1790-1802 (Brunswick and Mecklenburgh Squares, -0.1215/51.5240); Gordon Square and Woburn Square 1820s-1850s; Fitzroy Square 1794-1798 (-0.1390/51.5232). The Bedford estate closed its streets with gates and beadles until 1893.
sources: Survey of London vol 24 and the Bloomsbury volumes; British History Online
Wikipedia: Bloomsbury; Bedford Square; Russell Square

zones.name: Islington, Pentonville, Barnsbury, Canonbury and Highbury
zones.notes: The first big MIDDLE-CLASS suburb, built up the hill north of the New Road once Henry Penton began Pentonville in 1773 (-0.1140/51.5330) and the Regent's Canal (1812-20) and later the railways made the fields valuable. Highbury Place 1774-79 (-0.1013/51.5510); Canonbury Square 1805-30 (-0.0985/51.5432); Barnsbury/Cloudesley and Thornhill Squares 1820s-1850s (-0.1150/51.5412); Islington's population went from 10,200 in 1801 to 37,300 in 1831 and 95,300 in 1851. Stock-brick terraces and paired villas, generally lower and plainer than the West End.
sources: Survey of London vol 47 (Northern Clerkenwell and Pentonville)

zones.name: Knightsbridge, Brompton, Hans Town and Chelsea
zones.notes: Hans Town was laid out for Lord Cadogan by Henry Holland from 1777 - Sloane Street (-0.1590/51.4970), Hans Place, Cadogan Place - the first big development south-west of Hyde Park Corner. Riverside Chelsea was already a Tudor and Stuart village of some grandeur (Chelsea Royal Hospital 1682-92, -0.1600/51.4870; Cheyne Walk 1708-20, -0.1690/51.4832); Brompton and the Old Brompton Road stayed nursery gardens until the 1840s. Note Hyde Park (142 ha) and Kensington Gardens (111 ha) to the north are permanent voids from 1637 and 1728.

zones.name: St George's Fields, Newington, Kennington and Walworth
zones.notes: South London is a bridge story. Westminster Bridge opened 1750 and Blackfriars 1769, ending London Bridge's 600-year monopoly; new turnpikes were driven across the open St George's Fields and the fields were built over in one generation. The Elephant and Castle junction (-0.1000/51.4950) formed at the crossing of six new roads by 1780; Kennington (-0.1080/51.4840), Walworth (-0.0900/51.4870) and Newington filled 1790-1840 with modest 2-3 storey brick terraces and, on the better roads, semi-detached villas. Waterloo Bridge 1817, Southwark Bridge 1819, Vauxhall Bridge 1816 and the rebuilt London Bridge 1831 completed the frame.
sources: Survey of London vol 25 (St George the Martyr Southwark and St Mary Newington)
Wikipedia: Elephant and Castle; St George's Fields

zones.name: Bermondsey and Rotherhithe - leather, docks and the Surrey Canal
zones.notes: The Surrey Commercial Docks grew on the Howland Great Wet Dock from 1807 (Greenland Dock -0.0480/51.4920), the Grand Surrey Canal opened 1807 to Camberwell (1810) and Peckham (1826), and Bermondsey became the national centre of the leather trade (Bermondsey Leather Market 1833, -0.0808/51.4988) plus food processing, glue, and Peek Frean's biscuits from 1857. Tightly packed courts and yards between the tanyards - Jacob's Island (-0.0705/51.5010) was the most notorious slum in London and the setting for Bill Sikes's death in Oliver Twist (1838).
sources: Survey of London vol 26 (St Mary Bermondsey)
Wikipedia: Bermondsey; Surrey Commercial Docks; Jacob's Island

zones.name: Lambeth, Vauxhall, Stockwell and Clapham road ribbons
zones.notes: Ribbon development along Kennington Road, Clapham Road and Wandsworth Road after Westminster Bridge (1750) and Vauxhall Bridge (1816). Lambeth itself was a riverside industrial strip - Coade stone 1769, Doulton pottery 1815 (-0.1200/51.4930), Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens 1661-1859 (-0.1240/51.4855, a VOID until 1859) - while Clapham Common (89 ha, -0.1480/51.4610) and its ring of merchant villas held the 'Clapham Sect' from the 1790s. Keep density low: fields between the roads until the railways arrive in the 1860s.
sources: Survey of London vol 23 (South Bank and Vauxhall); vol 26

zones.name: Somers Town, Camden Town and Kentish Town
zones.notes: The first breach of the New Road line. Lord Somers began Somers Town in 1786 (-0.1305/51.5300, Clarendon Square), taking French emigres after 1789 and going downhill fast; Charles Pratt, 1st Earl Camden, laid out Camden Town from 1791 (-0.1425/51.5390) along the Hampstead Road; Kentish Town (-0.1400/51.5500) followed in the 1810s-1840s. The Regent's Canal (1812-20) and then the railway termini - Euston 1837 (-0.1330/51.5282), King's Cross 1852 (-0.1237/51.5308), St Pancras 1868 (-0.1263/51.5300) - drove viaducts, goods yards and coal drops straight through the district and turned much of it into slum by 1860.
sources: Survey of London vol 24; VCH Middlesex vol 9 (St Pancras)
Wikipedia: Somers Town, London; Camden Town

zones.name: Camberwell, Peckham, Brixton and Stockwell - the Georgian villa fringe
zones.notes: LOW-DENSITY ZONE: this should read as ribbons of detached and semi-detached stucco villas along the turnpikes with fields, nurseries and market gardens between - not solid streets. Camberwell Grove and Camberwell Green (-0.0930/51.4740); Brixton after Camberwell New Road 1818 and Brixton Road; Stockwell; Peckham Rye; Denmark Hill; Herne Hill 1820s. Camberwell parish had 7,000 people in 1801, 39,900 in 1841, and 259,300 by 1901 - the classic three-stage south London sequence of villa fringe, then Victorian terraces, then late-Victorian bye-law grid.
sources: Dyos, Victorian Suburb: a study of the growth of Camberwell (1961)

zones.name: Haggerston, Kingsland, De Beauvoir Town and Hoxton
zones.notes: The Regent's Canal (opened 1820) cut across here and pulled gasworks, timber wharves and furniture workshops with it. De Beauvoir Town (-0.0790/51.5390) was laid out on a square-within-a-square plan from 1821 and half built before the developer's lease collapsed in 1834; Haggerston and Hoxton filled with cheap terraces and courts. Densities were extreme by 1850: Shoreditch had over 350 people per hectare.

zones.name: The enclosed docks and their warehouse quarters
zones.notes: Between 1799 and 1828 Parliament authorised a ring of walled enclosed docks to stop river theft, and they rebuilt the whole east London waterfront in one generation: West India Docks 1800-02 (-0.0200/51.5085, the north edge of the Isle of Dogs), London Docks 1801-05 (-0.0620/51.5075, Wapping), East India Docks 1803-06 (-0.0060/51.5085, Blackwall), Surrey Commercial 1807 south of the river, St Katharine Docks 1825-28 (-0.0720/51.5065, which required demolishing 1,250 houses and displacing 11,300 people - the first great London clearance). DENSITY IS LOW because the dock basins themselves are water: build 6-8 storey brick warehouse walls around the rims. The rest of the Isle of Dogs stayed empty marsh until the 1840s.
sources: Survey of London vols 43-44 (Poplar, Blackwall and the Isle of Dogs)
Wikipedia: London Docks; West India Docks; St Katharine Docks

zones.name: Paddington, Tyburnia and the canal basin
zones.notes: The Paddington arm of the Grand Junction Canal opened in 1801 with its basin at -0.1750/51.5185, then the Bishop of London's estate was laid out as 'Tyburnia' from about 1824 - Connaught Square 1828 (-0.1650/51.5138), Sussex Gardens, Hyde Park Square - and Paddington station arrived 1838, rebuilt by Brunel 1854 (-0.1759/51.5164). Stucco-fronted Italianate terraces rather than plain brick: this is where the London kit changes from brown brick to white stucco, around 1825-1830. Paddington's population rose from 1,900 in 1801 to 46,300 in 1851.
sources: Survey of London vol 45? / VCH Middlesex vol 9 (Paddington)

zones.name: Regent's Park terraces and the Regent Street improvement
zones.notes: John Nash's scheme for the Crown on the old Marylebone Park: the park itself (166 ha, opened to the public 1835 - a VOID, do not build it) ringed by stucco palace-fronted terraces - Cornwall Terrace 1821, York Terrace, Cumberland Terrace 1826 (-0.1462/51.5320), Chester Terrace 1825, Park Crescent 1812-21 (-0.1450/51.5220) - plus eight planned villas of which a few were built. Linked to Carlton House by Regent Street, cut 1814-1825 along the social fault line between Mayfair and Soho, London's first modern street improvement and its first deliberate act of social zoning. Density is deliberately LOW: this is a ring of terrace, not a filled block.
sources: Survey of London; Crown Estate records
Wikipedia: Regent's Park; Regent Street; John Nash

zones.name: Belgravia - Cubitt on the Five Fields
zones.notes: The Grosvenor family's second estate, on the swampy 'Five Fields' south of Hyde Park Corner, drained and raised with spoil from the St Katharine Docks excavation of 1826-28. Thomas Cubitt built it as a single vertically integrated operation from 1825: Belgrave Square 1826-37 (-0.1533/51.4989, by George Basevi), Eaton Square 1826-55 (-0.1533/51.4958, the largest garden square in London), Chester Square 1840. White or cream stucco, giant porticoes, 5-6 storeys - the peak of Regency terrace grandeur, and the moment London's most expensive address moves from Mayfair to Belgravia.
sources: Survey of London vols 39-40 (The Grosvenor Estate)
Wikipedia: Belgravia; Thomas Cubitt; Belgrave Square

zones.name: St John's Wood, Maida Vale, Kilburn and West Hampstead
zones.notes: St John's Wood (-0.1720/51.5330) was laid out from 1794 and built 1820-1850 as the FIRST fully semi-detached villa suburb in the world - the prototype for every English suburb since, and the reason 'semi-detached' is the default London housing kit. Lord's cricket ground here from 1814 (-0.1729/51.5299, a void). Maida Vale's Italianate mansion flats followed 1860-1900; Kilburn High Road (-0.1930/51.5470) and West Hampstead were built after the Metropolitan (1879) and Midland lines. Regent's Park barracks, Paddington Recreation Ground and Kilburn Grange are voids.
sources: Survey of London; VCH Middlesex vol 9
Wikipedia: St John's Wood; Maida Vale; Kilburn, London

zones.name: Pimlico
zones.notes: Cubitt's third estate, on the low marshy Neat House market gardens between Belgravia and the river, built from 1835 to the 1860s on ground raised several feet. Warwick Square (-0.1400/51.4900), Eccleston Square, St George's Square 1839-50s (-0.1367/51.4885, the only London square open to the river). Same stucco kit as Belgravia but thinner, narrower and one social rung down - it was lodging-house London by 1880. Victoria station arrived 1860 (-0.1441/51.4952) and the Thames Embankment work of 1864-70 finally fixed the river wall.

zones.name: Bayswater, Notting Hill and the Ladbroke estate
zones.notes: The great stucco belt. Bayswater and Westbourne Grove built 1840-1860 north of Kensington Gardens; the Ladbroke estate laid out 1823 as a hippodrome racecourse, re-planned 1840s and built 1845-1870 as concentric crescents around communal garden squares (Ladbroke Square -0.2032/51.5108, Stanley Crescent, Lansdowne Crescent) - the finest planned landscape of Victorian London. Notting Hill Gate -0.1966/51.5090. The Metropolitan Railway reached Paddington in 1863 and Notting Hill Gate in 1868. The Potteries and Piggeries slum at Notting Dale (-0.2110/51.5130) survived inside this genteel zone until the 1890s.
sources: Wikipedia: Notting Hill; Ladbroke Estate; Bayswater

zones.name: Poplar, Millwall and Cubitt Town on the Isle of Dogs
zones.notes: The Isle of Dogs was empty marsh until the 1840s. William Cubitt began Cubitt Town on the east side in 1843 (-0.0110/51.4930); Millwall on the west took shipyards and ironworks including John Scott Russell's yard, where Brunel's Great Eastern was built and launched sideways in 1858 (-0.0230/51.4920). Poplar High Street and the East India Dock Road filled with dockers' terraces; Blackwall, Cubitt Town and Millwall by 1890 were a continuous industrial-residential mass wrapped around dock water. This is the polygon that later becomes the Docklands dereliction zone of 1967-81 and then Canary Wharf.
sources: Survey of London vols 43-44 (Poplar, Blackwall and the Isle of Dogs)
Wikipedia: Isle of Dogs; Cubitt Town; Millwall

zones.name: Hampstead, Belsize Park, Swiss Cottage and Gospel Oak
zones.notes: Hampstead village (-0.1780/51.5560) was already a spa and merchant retreat by 1700; the Victorian growth is the Belsize and Eton College estates 1850-1880, built as detached and semi-detached Italianate villas in large gardens - hence density only 0.55, much lower than the East End. Hampstead Heath (-0.1650/51.5600, 320 ha) was saved by Act of Parliament in 1871 after a 40-year legal war with the lord of the manor and is the largest permanent void in north London: mark it, because the 1871 Act is why the built-up area has a hole here forever.

zones.name: The City rebuilt as an office district; the Victorian street improvements
zones.notes: Not outward growth but total internal replacement. The City's resident population collapsed from 128,800 in 1801 to 128,000 in 1851, 51,400 in 1881 and 26,900 in 1901 as houses were replaced by banks, insurance offices, warehouses and railway termini. The Bank of England, Royal Exchange 1844, Coal Exchange 1849, Leadenhall Market 1881, Smithfield Market 1868, plus the great new streets - see events.json for the clearance polygons of New Oxford Street 1847, Victoria Street 1851, Holborn Viaduct 1869, Queen Victoria Street 1871, Shaftesbury Avenue and Charing Cross Road 1886-87 and Kingsway 1900-05. Height rises from 3-4 storeys to 5-7; the London Building Act 1894 caps buildings at 80 ft plus two storeys of roof, and that cap holds until 1954.
sources: Wikipedia: City of London; London Building Act 1894

zones.name: Detached outer railway towns - Richmond, Twickenham, Kingston, Surbiton, Wimbledon, Barnet, Bromley, Sutton, Enfield, Uxbridge
zones.notes: IMPORTANT MODELLING NOTE: this polygon only covers the Richmond-Kingston-Surbiton-Wimbledon group. The other detached Victorian towns are NOT contiguous with London and should be seeded from villages.json as separate patches with these dates: Surbiton from 1838 (the LSWR's own new town, -0.3040/51.3920); Richmond 1846; Twickenham 1848; Wimbledon 1838, 41,700 people by 1901; New Malden 1846; Barnet 1850s; Bromley 1858, 33,600 by 1911; Sutton 1847, 17,700 by 1901; Enfield; Uxbridge; Watford; Epsom. Each grew as a compact plug around its station 800-1500 m across, separated by open farmland from London and from each other until the interwar sprawl of 1920-39 welded them together.

zones.name: Kentish Town, Tufnell Park, Holloway and Archway
zones.notes: Solid terrace London, built by small builders on 99-year leases 1845-1890 and hemmed by railways on every side (Midland 1868, North London 1850, Great Northern 1850). Holloway Road -0.1150/51.5530; Tufnell Park -0.1380/51.5570; Archway -0.1350/51.5655. Mr Pooter's 'The Laurels, Brickfield Terrace, Holloway' in Diary of a Nobody (1892) is the definitive literary portrait of this kit: 6-room brick terrace, bay window, tiny front garden, clerk's family. Highgate Cemetery 1839 (-0.1470/51.5670) and Waterlow Park are voids.

zones.name: Hackney, Dalston, London Fields, Homerton and Victoria Park
zones.notes: Hackney's population went from 38,000 in 1841 to 199,000 in 1891. The North London Railway (1850) and cheap workmen's fares turned the old villages of Dalston (-0.0750/51.5460), Hackney (-0.0550/51.5470), Homerton and De Beauvoir into a continuous grid of 2-storey terraces and small workshops (furniture, shoes, clothing). Victoria Park, opened 1845 after a Chartist petition, was the first purpose-built public park for the East End (-0.0400/51.5360, 86 ha) - a void, and a deliberate act of social policy after the 1832 cholera epidemic. London Fields (-0.0620/51.5410) and Hackney Downs are voids.
sources: Wikipedia: Hackney, London; Victoria Park, London

zones.name: Bow, Bromley-by-Bow, Stratford, West Ham, Plaistow, Canning Town and Silvertown
zones.notes: The industrial East End beyond the River Lea, outside the Metropolitan Board of Works and therefore outside its building regulations, which is exactly why the noxious trades went there. Stratford (-0.0030/51.5420) got the Eastern Counties Railway works in 1847 (which built the town of 'Stratford New Town'); Thames Ironworks at Bow Creek from 1846; the Royal Victoria Dock 1855 (0.0180/51.5080), Royal Albert 1880 (0.0490/51.5090), Beckton gasworks 1870 (0.0680/51.5170, the largest in the world); Tate's sugar at Silvertown 1878 (0.0400/51.5030) and Keiller's, Brunner Mond (site of the 1917 Silvertown explosion). West Ham's population went from 18,800 in 1851 to 267,400 in 1901. Kit: the plainest possible bye-law terrace, plus vast factory sheds and gasholders.
sources: Wikipedia: West Ham; Silvertown; Royal Docks

zones.name: Camberwell, Peckham, Brixton, Herne Hill and Dulwich fringe
zones.notes: H. J. Dyos's Camberwell is the best-documented Victorian suburb in the world: 39,900 people in 1841, 111,300 in 1871, 259,300 in 1901, built plot by plot by hundreds of tiny speculative builders each putting up two to six houses. Brixton (-0.1150/51.4620) got London's first purpose-built department street and, after the 1880 electric-lit Electric Avenue, the classic high-street kit. Peckham (-0.0690/51.4740), Herne Hill, Denmark Hill, Loughborough Junction. Dulwich stayed low-density because the Dulwich College estate refused to sell freeholds - Dulwich Park (1890) and the Dulwich woods (-0.0800/51.4400) are voids and the reason there is a hole in the built-up area here.

zones.name: Deptford, Greenwich, Charlton, Woolwich and Plumstead
zones.notes: Government and industrial south-east London. Deptford royal dockyard closed 1869 and became the Foreign Cattle Market; the Royal Arsenal at Woolwich (0.0720/51.4920) employed 10,900 in 1886 and nearly 80,000 at the 1918 peak, and its housing spread over Plumstead (0.0850/51.4830) and Woolwich Common; Charlton and Greenwich Marsh took cable works (Enderby's, from which the first Atlantic cable was laid in 1865) and Siemens. Greenwich Park (-0.0010/51.4770, 74 ha, enclosed 1433) and Blackheath (0.0080/51.4680, 85 ha) and Woolwich Common are permanent voids; the Royal Naval Hospital / Greenwich Hospital (-0.0080/51.4830, 1696-1751) is the great monument here.
sources: Wikipedia: Royal Arsenal; Deptford Dockyard; Greenwich

zones.name: North Kensington, Kensal Town and Westbourne Park
zones.notes: Built fast and badly between the Great Western main line (1838) and the canal: Kensal Town (-0.2110/51.5250), Golborne, Notting Dale, Latimer Road. Kensal Green Cemetery opened 1833 (-0.2270/51.5280) is a permanent void. By Booth's 1889 maps this was 'very poor, chronic want' black and dark blue over most of the area, in direct contact with the wealthy Ladbroke crescents 400 m south - one of the sharpest social gradients in London and still visible today.
sources: Booth Poverty Map 1889 (Charles Booth Online Archive, LSE)

zones.name: Stoke Newington, Stamford Hill, Clapton and Highbury New Park
zones.notes: Middle-class then lower-middle-class terraces spreading up the Kingsland Road and the Hackney Brook valley. Highbury New Park 1853; Stoke Newington (-0.0760/51.5620) and Clapton (-0.0560/51.5620) filled 1860-1895. Abney Park Cemetery 1840 (-0.0760/51.5652), Clissold Park (1889) and the Stoke Newington and Walthamstow reservoirs (New River / East London Waterworks) are voids. The Lea marshes on the east edge (-0.0400/51.5650) were never built on and are now the Lee Valley Park.

zones.name: Norwood, Sydenham, Forest Hill, Penge and Crystal Palace
zones.notes: The Crystal Palace was re-erected on Sydenham Hill in 1852-54 (-0.0730/51.4225) and instantly created a hilltop suburb of large detached villas, served by two competing railways (LBSCR 1854, LCDR high-level 1865). Anerley, Penge, Upper and West Norwood, Forest Hill and Honor Oak filled 1860-1900, with density held down by the steep hills and big plots. The Palace burned on 30 November 1936 - a small but visually spectacular event for the timelapse. Norwood, Nunhead (1840) and Crystal Palace Park are voids.
sources: Wikipedia: Crystal Palace, London; Sydenham; Penge

zones.name: South Kensington, Earl's Court and West Brompton
zones.notes: The Great Exhibition profit of 1851 bought the 87-acre Albertopolis estate (-0.1750/51.4970: V&A 1857-1909, Natural History Museum 1873-81, Science Museum, Royal Albert Hall 1867-71, Imperial College). Around it the Gunter, Day and Alexander estates built enormous red-brick and stucco terraces 1860-1890: Onslow Square, The Boltons 1850s (-0.1840/51.4880), Earl's Court after the District line station of 1871 (-0.1940/51.4917), West Brompton and Redcliffe Square. Brompton Cemetery 1840 (-0.1880/51.4855) is a void.

zones.name: Croydon, Thornton Heath, South Norwood, Selhurst and Addiscombe
zones.notes: Croydon was an ancient market town and archbishop's manor 15 km from the City, and it became the biggest free-standing town in the London region: 20,300 people in 1851, 133,900 in 1901, 190,900 in 1931. The London and Croydon Railway (1839) and then the LBSCR made it commuter territory, and it built its own Town Hall (1896), tramway (1901) and, from 1920, London's airport (-0.1130/51.3560, closed 1959). At this date Croydon is still a DETACHED town with green fields between it and Streatham - do not merge it into the continuous built-up mass until about 1930.

zones.name: Battersea, Clapham, Wandsworth, Putney and Earlsfield
zones.notes: Battersea grew from 6,600 in 1841 to 168,900 in 1901 - almost all of it after Clapham Junction opened in 1863, which became and remains the busiest railway junction in Britain (-0.1704/51.4644). The Shaftesbury Park Estate 1872-77 (-0.1610/51.4665, 1,200 houses by the Artizans, Labourers and General Dwellings Company) was the first big philanthropic model suburb. Battersea Park was laid out on Battersea Fields 1854-58 (-0.1600/51.4790, 80 ha, a void). Wandsworth and Putney kept a lower density on the hills; Wandsworth Common, Clapham Common (89 ha), Putney Heath and Wimbledon Common (460 ha, saved 1871) are voids.
sources: Wikipedia: Battersea; Clapham Junction; Shaftesbury Park Estate

zones.name: New Cross, Brockley, Lewisham, Hither Green and Catford
zones.notes: Railway suburbia in the Ravensbourne valley: New Cross 1849, Brockley 1871 (-0.0370/51.4640), Ladywell, Lewisham (-0.0110/51.4620), Hither Green 1895, Catford 1892 (-0.0210/51.4450). Cameron Corbett's St German's estate at Brockley/Hither Green (1896-1914) sold 3,000 temperance houses (no pubs allowed in the leases) to City clerks. Density 0.75 because a good deal of this is generous bay-fronted terrace and semi with gardens rather than solid grid. Blackheath, Hilly Fields (1896), Ladywell Fields and Beckenham Place Park are voids.
sources: Wikipedia: Brockley; Catford; Archibald Cameron Corbett

zones.name: Hammersmith, Shepherd's Bush, West Kensington and Brook Green
zones.notes: Hammersmith Broadway -0.2240/51.4927, Shepherd's Bush Green -0.2190/51.5052. The Hammersmith and City Railway opened 1864, the District reached Hammersmith 1874, and the fields between the old riverside village and Kensington filled solidly by 1900. West Kensington and Barons Court were built 1877-1900 by Sir William Palliser and the Gunter estate. Wormwood Scrubs (-0.2320/51.5200, 80 ha, common land from 1879) is a permanent void; the 1908 Franco-British Exhibition and Olympic stadium at White City (-0.2240/51.5120) filled the last big gap.

zones.name: Finsbury Park, Stroud Green, Crouch End, Hornsey and Muswell Hill
zones.notes: Suburban growth pulled up the Great Northern branches. Finsbury Park opened as a public park in 1869 (-0.1060/51.5665, 45 ha, a void) and its station in 1861; Crouch End (-0.1220/51.5790) and Hornsey (-0.1200/51.5870) filled 1880-1900; Muswell Hill (-0.1440/51.5900) was built almost entirely 1896-1914 by one man, James Edmondson, and is the most complete Edwardian suburb in London. Alexandra Palace and Park 1873 (-0.1300/51.5940, 80 ha) is a void.
sources: Wikipedia: Muswell Hill; Crouch End; Finsbury Park

zones.name: Chiswick, Acton, Ealing and Brentford
zones.notes: 'Queen of the Suburbs': Ealing (-0.3020/51.5150) was deliberately built as a high-class detached and semi-detached suburb 1878-1914 under strict covenants, reaching 61,200 people by 1911; Acton (-0.2730/51.5085) went the other way and became 'Soapsuds Island', with 170 laundries by 1900 washing the West End's linen, plus the district's terraces for the laundresses. Chiswick and Bedford Park (-0.2570/51.4940) - Jonathan Carr's estate of 1875-86 by Norman Shaw - was the FIRST garden suburb in the world and the source of the red-brick, white-woodwork, Dutch-gable kit that the whole interwar suburb later copies.

zones.name: Fulham, Walham Green, Parsons Green and Sands End
zones.notes: Market gardens and nurseries until the 1870s, then the fastest-growing part of west London: Fulham's population went from 23,400 in 1871 to 91,600 in 1891 and 137,300 in 1901. Grid after grid of two-storey bye-law terraces built under the Metropolitan Board of Works and then the 1875 Public Health Act standards. Fulham Broadway (Walham Green) station 1880 (-0.1948/51.4802); Fulham Palace and Bishop's Park (-0.2130/51.4715) and Hurlingham (-0.2080/51.4690) are voids.

zones.name: Tottenham, Wood Green, Edmonton and Bruce Grove
zones.notes: THE workmen's-train suburb. The Great Eastern Railway was compelled by its 1864 Act to run twopenny workmen's trains on the Enfield and Walthamstow lines, and the Cheap Trains Act 1883 forced more; the result was a flood of the poorest clerks and artisans out of the East End into Tottenham (-0.0680/51.5880) and Edmonton (-0.0600/51.6150), which grew from 13,200 (Tottenham, 1871) to 102,500 in 1901. Small, cheap, uniform bye-law terraces - the densest and plainest Victorian kit in London. Wood Green (-0.1090/51.5970) was slightly better class after the 1859 station. Tottenham Marshes and the Lea reservoirs on the east edge are voids.

zones.name: Walthamstow, Leyton, Leytonstone and Wanstead fringe
zones.notes: The same workmen's-fare mechanism as Tottenham, on the other Great Eastern line. Walthamstow's population went from 11,100 in 1871 to 95,100 in 1901 (a 750 percent rise in 30 years - the fastest sustained growth of any London district ever recorded); Leyton from 4,900 in 1861 to 98,900 in 1901. Endless streets of identical 2-up-2-down terraces laid out on the field boundaries. Epping Forest was saved by the Epping Forest Act 1878 (-0.0100/51.6200 northwards, 2,400 ha) and Wanstead Flats (0.0150/51.5560) with it - the hardest permanent northern edge in the model.
sources: Wikipedia: Walthamstow; Leyton; Epping Forest Act 1878

zones.name: Balham, Tooting, Streatham, Norbury and Mitcham fringe
zones.notes: The last big Victorian and Edwardian push in south London, delivered by the LBSCR and the electric trams. Balham (-0.1520/51.4430), Tooting (-0.1680/51.4270), Streatham (-0.1300/51.4270), Norbury. The LCC's Totterdown Fields estate at Tooting, 1901-11 (-0.1660/51.4300, 1,229 cottages) was the first LCC 'out-county' cottage estate and the direct ancestor of Becontree - a genuinely dateable turning point in what London builds. Tooting Bec and Tooting Graveney Commons and Streatham Common are voids.
sources: LCC Housing of the Working Classes 1855-1912

zones.name: Willesden, Harlesden, Kensal Rise, Cricklewood and Neasden
zones.notes: Railway-worker London: Willesden Junction (1866) and the LNWR, Midland and Great Central lines converged here and Willesden's population went from 3,900 in 1861 to 114,800 in 1901 and 154,200 in 1911 - proportionally one of the biggest Victorian jumps anywhere. Harlesden (-0.2480/51.5360), Kensal Rise, Cricklewood (-0.2130/51.5560), Neasden depot 1882. Modest bay-fronted terraces plus railway sidings and, from 1900, the first big factories on the Edgware Road.

zones.name: East Ham, Forest Gate, Manor Park, Barking and Ilford
zones.notes: The eastern frontier of Victorian London. East Ham grew from 9,700 (1881) to 96,000 (1901); Ilford from 7,600 (1881) to 41,200 (1901) and 78,200 (1911), largely as the Cameron Corbett 'Ilford Garden Suburb' estates of 1898-1910 (0.0700/51.5620) - bay-fronted terraces sold to City clerks on the Great Eastern. Barking (0.0810/51.5390) was an ancient fishing town swallowed in the same wave. Wanstead Flats and City of London Cemetery (0.0350/51.5570) are voids.
sources: Wikipedia: Ilford; East Ham; Archibald Cameron Corbett

zones.name: Edwardian infill and the first LCC cottage estates, 1900-1914
zones.notes: COARSE OUTER ENVELOPE - use it only to close the last Victorian and Edwardian gaps, NOT to fill the interior; only about 55 percent of the cells inside it are built by 1915 (Hampstead Heath, Epping Forest, Wimbledon Common, Richmond Park, the Lea and Thames marshes, the Dulwich and Hendon farmland, and the gaps between the detached towns are still open). By 1914 the continuous built-up area reached roughly Golders Green (Northern line extension 1907), Muswell Hill, Wood Green, Walthamstow, Ilford, Barking, Woolwich, Catford, Streatham, Tooting, Wimbledon, Richmond, Ealing and Willesden - about 450-500 km2 all told, with Croydon, Bromley, Sutton, Kingston, Enfield, Barnet, Romford and Uxbridge still detached towns beyond it. Key Edwardian additions: the LCC's first out-county cottage estates (Totterdown Fields 1903-11, White Hart Lane / Tower Gardens 1904-15, Old Oak 1911-13, Norbury 1906); Hampstead Garden Suburb from 1907 (-0.1930/51.5790, Henrietta Barnett with Parker and Unwin), which sets the low-density template for the whole interwar era; the deep tube extensions of 1906-07 (Bakerloo, Piccadilly, Hampstead lines) and the LCC electric trams of 1901-14.
sources: Wikipedia: Hampstead Garden Suburb; London County Council housing

zones.name: Eltham, Well Hall, New Eltham, Mottingham, Kidbrooke and Falconwood
zones.notes: Starts EARLY: the Well Hall / Progress Estate at Eltham was built by the Government in just under a year in 1915 (0.0430/51.4570, 1,298 houses by Frank Baines) to house Woolwich Arsenal munition workers, and it is the finest and most influential state housing scheme in Britain - the direct model for the whole 1919 cottage-estate programme. Around it, Woolwich Borough's own Page estate 1920s and vast private estates 1928-1939 covered Eltham (0.0520/51.4520), Mottingham, New Eltham and Falconwood. Eltham Palace (0.0530/51.4490, medieval; Courtauld house 1933-36) and Avery Hill and Oxleas Wood are voids.

zones.name: Interwar inner infill - mansion blocks, LCC blocks and the arterial-road factories
zones.notes: LOW-DENSITY OVERLAY on the already-built inner area: use it to replace, not to add. Three things happen inside the Victorian city between the wars. (1) Blocks of flats: LCC five-storey balcony-access estates on cleared slum sites, and private mansion blocks in Kensington, Marylebone and St John's Wood. (2) Arterial roads and the factories along them - the North Circular 1921-34, Western Avenue A40 from 1921, the Great West Road 1925 with its 'Golden Mile' of Art Deco factories at Brentford (-0.3050/51.4880: Firestone 1928, Gillette 1936, Coty), the Great Cambridge Road 1924, Eastern Avenue 1925, Kingston By-Pass 1927 (Britain's first). (3) Cinemas, Tube stations by Charles Holden 1926-1935, and pubs. Height: 4-6 storeys, brick with concrete trim.
sources: Wikipedia: North Circular Road; Great West Road; Charles Holden

zones.name: The 1939 built-up envelope
zones.notes: COARSE ENVELOPE for the whole interwar period - use only to catch anything the district zones above miss, at low priority. Between 1919 and 1939 Greater London's population rose from about 7.4 million to 8.6 million but its built-up area roughly DOUBLED, from about 500 km2 to about 1,000-1,100 km2, because the new suburbs were built at 8-12 houses per acre against the Victorian 40-60. Roughly 860,000 dwellings were built in the London region in those twenty years, about three-quarters of them privately for owner-occupation on 25-year mortgages at 450-900 pounds a house. This is the largest and fastest physical growth event in London's history and should be the visual climax of the timelapse - a green ring turning grey in about 15 seconds of screen time.

zones.name: Golders Green, Hendon, Colindale, Burnt Oak and Edgware
zones.notes: The archetype of Northern-line suburbia. The Hampstead tube reached Golders Green in 1907 (-0.1940/51.5720), Hendon Central 1923 (-0.2270/51.5830), Colindale and Burnt Oak 1924 (-0.2650/51.6020), Edgware 18 Aug 1924 (-0.2750/51.6130) - built into open fields, with the developers following within two years. Hendon's population rose from 57,600 in 1921 to 115,700 in 1931 and about 155,000 by 1939. The LCC's Watling estate at Burnt Oak, 1926-31 (-0.2620/51.6030, 4,034 houses), is the big public block inside the private tide. Kit: bay-fronted, gabled, pebble-dashed or half-timbered SEMI-DETACHED pairs on 25-30 ft frontages, 8-12 houses per acre - the single most important building kit for the whole 1920-39 act.
sources: Wikipedia: Edgware tube station; Watling Estate; Hendon

zones.name: Southall, Hayes, Yiewsley, Hillingdon and Uxbridge
zones.notes: Industrial Metro-land rather than commuter Metro-land: the Grand Union Canal and the GWR gave Hayes and Southall a factory belt - HMV/EMI at Hayes from 1907 (-0.4180/51.5100), Nestle 1913, Fairey Aviation, AEC bus works at Southall 1926 (-0.3720/51.5020) - and the housing followed the jobs. Hayes and Harlington UD grew from 9,000 in 1921 to 44,000 by 1939. Uxbridge (-0.4780/51.5460) was an ancient market town; the Metropolitan and District arrived in 1904 and the Piccadilly took over in 1933.

zones.name: Finchley, Mill Hill, Friern Barnet, Whetstone and Barnet
zones.notes: The Northern line's other arm. The Great Northern branch to Finchley (1867) and High Barnet (1872) was taken over by the Underground in 1940 under the 1935-40 New Works Programme, but the housing had already gone up on the strength of the steam service and the buses: Finchley (-0.1870/51.5990) 39,400 people in 1921, 58,900 in 1931; Mill Hill (-0.2320/51.6150) and Whetstone (-0.1780/51.6280) built 1928-1938; Friern Barnet, East Barnet and New Barnet 1925-1939. Growth here stops abruptly at the 1938 Green Belt line north of Barnet - the sharpest surviving edge in the model. Totteridge (-0.2100/51.6320) stayed open and still is.
sources: VCH Middlesex vol 6 (Finchley, Friern Barnet, Hendon)
Wikipedia: Finchley; Northern line New Works Programme

zones.name: Palmers Green, Southgate, Winchmore Hill, Cockfosters, Oakwood and Enfield
zones.notes: Palmers Green (-0.1090/51.6180) was built out from 1902-1914 on the Great Northern branch; the big wave came with the Piccadilly line extension of 1932-33 - Arnos Grove (19 Sep 1932), Southgate (13 Mar 1933, -0.1280/51.6320), Oakwood and Cockfosters (31 Jul 1933, -0.1490/51.6520) - all Charles Holden stations built deliberately AHEAD of the houses, with the estates following in 1933-1938. Enfield (-0.0810/51.6520) was an old market town with the Royal Small Arms Factory (1816) and Ediswan/Ferguson works. The Green Belt line stops everything north of about 51.665.
sources: Wikipedia: Piccadilly line; Southgate tube station; Enfield Town

zones.name: Edmonton north, Chingford, Highams Park and Woodford
zones.notes: The last of the Lea-valley belt. Chingford (-0.0100/51.6320) and Highams Park filled 1925-1938; Woodford, South Woodford and Woodford Green (0.0270/51.6070) grew on the Great Eastern line, taken into the Central line only in 1947-48. Growth is hard-stopped on the east by EPPING FOREST (2,400 ha, saved by the Epping Forest Act 1878, City of London Corporation as conservators) and on the west by the Lea Valley reservoirs (King George V Reservoir 1913, William Girling 1951) - two of the most important permanent voids in the model.
sources: Wikipedia: Chingford; Epping Forest; Lee Valley Park

zones.name: Ilford outer, Gants Hill, Barkingside, Newbury Park and Wanstead
zones.notes: Eastern Avenue (A12) was opened in 1925 straight across the Essex fields and the houses went up beside it within five years. Ilford MB population: 85,200 in 1921, 131,100 in 1931, about 180,000 by 1939. Gants Hill (0.0660/51.5760), Barkingside (0.0870/51.5860), Newbury Park and Seven Kings. The Central line extension along the old Great Eastern Fairlop Loop was authorised in 1935-36 but delayed by the war and opened 1947-48, so the houses came a decade before the tube here - the reverse of the Cockfosters case. Hainault Forest and Fairlop Plain are voids.
sources: Wikipedia: Ilford; Gants Hill tube station; Eastern Avenue

zones.name: Croydon outer - Shirley, Addiscombe, Sanderstead, Purley and Coulsdon
zones.notes: Croydon Corporation and the Southern Railway between them turned the chalk downland south and east of the town into suburb 1922-1939: Shirley (-0.0570/51.3720), Addington, Sanderstead (-0.0810/51.3370), Purley (-0.1120/51.3370), Coulsdon (-0.1380/51.3210), Selsdon (electrified 1935). Croydon CB population 190,900 in 1931, about 250,000 by 1939. Crucially, this is where the built-up area finally MERGES with the Streatham/Norbury edge, so that from about 1930 Croydon is no longer a detached town. Croydon Airport 1920-1959 (-0.1130/51.3560) is the great landmark here; Addington Hills, Farthing Downs and Riddlesdown are voids.

zones.name: Becontree - the largest public housing estate in the world
zones.notes: The single biggest discrete addition to London's built-up area in its whole history. Built by the London County Council under the Housing and Town Planning Act 1919 ('Homes fit for Heroes') on about 3,000 acres / 1,200 ha of Essex market garden compulsorily purchased across Barking, Dagenham and Ilford. Construction ran 1921-1935 (first tenants 1921); about 26,000-27,000 houses for 115,000-120,000 people at 12 houses to the acre, with its own construction railway from a jetty on the Thames. Cottage-estate kit: brick or rendered terraces of 4-6 and semi-detached pairs, hipped roofs, front and back gardens, wide grass-verged roads on a Parker-and-Unwin-derived layout, and famously almost no pubs, shops or jobs at first. Ford opened its Dagenham plant in 1931 alongside it (0.1450/51.5250) and gave the estate its economy.
sources: LCC Housing reports; Becontree 100 (RIBA / Google Arts and Culture)
londonshoes.blog Becontree centenary; Municipal Borough of Dagenham

zones.name: Wembley, Wembley Park, Kingsbury, Preston Road, Sudbury and Alperton
zones.notes: Metro-land proper: the Metropolitan Railway was the only British railway allowed to own and develop land, and its Metropolitan Railway Country Estates Ltd built nine estates along the line from 1919, marketing them with the annual 'Metro-land' guide (first issued 1915). Wembley Park (-0.2790/51.5630) was the site of the British Empire Exhibition of 1924-25 with the Empire Stadium of 1923 (-0.2795/51.5560, the Twin Towers, demolished 2003). Wembley UD population: 16,200 in 1921, 48,500 in 1931, about 121,000 by 1939 - a seven-fold rise in 18 years, the fastest in Britain. Kingsbury (-0.2780/51.5840) was built 1928-1935, including the extraordinary 'Kingsbury eccentric' individualist houses on Buck Lane.
sources: Wikipedia: Metro-land; Wembley; British Empire Exhibition

zones.name: Harrow, Rayners Lane, Pinner, Eastcote, Ruislip and Northwood
zones.notes: The deepest Metro-land. Rayners Lane (-0.3710/51.5750) went from 22 passengers a year in 1930 to 4 million by 1937 as the Harrow Garden Village estate went up around it; Pinner (-0.3810/51.5930), Eastcote (-0.3970/51.5760), Ruislip Manor (-0.4120/51.5730) and Northwood (-0.4240/51.6110) all followed 1929-1937. Harrow's population: 49,100 in 1921, 96,700 in 1931, 190,000 by 1939. Ruislip's growth was partly restrained by the 1914 Ruislip-Northwood town-planning scheme, the first statutory planning scheme in Britain. Ruislip Woods and the Lido are voids.

zones.name: Perivale, Greenford, Northolt, South Harrow and Sudbury Hill
zones.notes: Western Avenue (A40, built in stages 1921-1943) brought both the houses and the Art Deco factories: the Hoover Building at Perivale, 1932-35 by Wallis Gilbert (-0.3200/51.5280), Sanderson's, Aladdin, Rockware Glass at Greenford. The Central line was extended over the GWR out to Greenford and West Ruislip only in 1947, so most of this growth was driven by road and by the Great Western's own suburban service. Greenford's population went from 900 in 1921 to 38,000 by 1939. Horsenden Hill, Northolt aerodrome (1915) and the Brent valley are voids.
sources: Wikipedia: Western Avenue, London; Hoover Building; Greenford

zones.name: Heston, Hounslow, Feltham, Whitton and Hanworth
zones.notes: The Great West Road (1925), the Piccadilly line extension to Hounslow West (1933) and the Southern Railway's electrification of the Windsor lines (1930) opened the Middlesex market gardens west of Isleworth. Heston, Hounslow (-0.3610/51.4680), Whitton (-0.3560/51.4530), Feltham (-0.4090/51.4490) and Hanworth were built out 1928-1939. Heston Aerodrome (1929) and Hanworth Air Park (1917) are here; Hounslow Heath and the reservoirs to the west are voids. The Great South-West Road and the future Heathrow (a Fairey airfield from 1930, requisitioned 1944, civil airport from 1946) lie just beyond the south-west corner.
sources: Wikipedia: Hounslow; Great West Road; Heathrow Airport

zones.name: Romford, Gidea Park, Hornchurch, Elm Park, Upminster and Rainham
zones.notes: The far eastern frontier, reached by the District line extension to Upminster (1932, over LMS tracks) and the widened Southend arterial road (A127, 1925). Romford (0.1830/51.5760) was a market town of 19,100 in 1921 and 35,900 in 1931; Gidea Park had the 1911 and 1934 model-housing exhibitions; Elm Park (0.1990/51.5490) was built as a complete new estate 1934-1939 with its own station opened 13 May 1935; Hornchurch (0.2190/51.5560) and Upminster (0.2510/51.5560) filled 1930-1939. Hornchurch aerodrome (RAF Hornchurch, 1915-1962, 0.2200/51.5340) and the Ingrebourne valley are voids.
sources: Wikipedia: Romford; Elm Park station; Upminster

zones.name: Welling, Bexleyheath, Barnehurst, Blackfen, Sidcup and Erith
zones.notes: 'Bexley' is the textbook case of unplanned interwar ribbon and estate sprawl: the Southern Railway electrified the Bexleyheath and Dartford Loop lines in 1926, and the New Ideal Homesteads company and its rivals covered the Kent orchards with cheap 375-pound semis, 1929-1939. Bexley UD population: 21,000 in 1921, 32,900 in 1931, 95,700 in 1939 - and Sidcup (0.1030/51.4270), Welling (0.1050/51.4640), Blackfen (0.1000/51.4550) and Barnehurst (0.1550/51.4690) are almost entirely a single decade's work, 1930-1939. Erith (0.1770/51.4820) is older and industrial (Vickers). This is the growth that provoked the Restriction of Ribbon Development Act 1935 and then the Green Belt.
sources: Wikipedia: Bexley; Bexleyheath; New Ideal Homesteads

zones.name: Beckenham, Bromley, Chislehurst, Petts Wood, Orpington and West Wickham
zones.notes: Southern Railway electrification (Bromley 1925-26, Orpington 1925) plus the Kent commuter market. Petts Wood (0.0740/51.3900) is the cleanest single example in London of a 1928-1935 speculative garden estate built around a station opened on 9 July 1928 specifically to serve it, developed by Basil Scruby with covenants controlling every detail. Bromley grew from 35,100 (1921) to 45,300 (1931) to about 70,000 (1939); Orpington UD from 10,700 (1921) to 45,000 (1939). Density is held at 0.55 because plots are large and there is a lot of retained woodland. Hayes Common, Chislehurst Common, High Elms and Petts Wood (National Trust, 1927) are voids.
sources: Wikipedia: Petts Wood; Orpington; Bromley, London

zones.name: Sutton, Cheam, Carshalton, Wallington, Worcester Park and Ewell
zones.notes: Electrification of the Southern's Sutton, Epsom and Wimbledon lines in 1925-1930 opened the last big block of Surrey farmland inside the future Greater London boundary. Sutton and Cheam MB population: 21,300 in 1921, 47,600 in 1931, 69,000 in 1939. Cheam (-0.2140/51.3600) and Stoneleigh (-0.2400/51.3630, station opened 17 July 1932 for the new estates, again ahead of the houses) are pure 1930s. Nonsuch Park, Oaks Park and the Banstead Downs beyond form the Green Belt edge.
sources: Wikipedia: Sutton, London; Stoneleigh railway station; Cheam

zones.name: Kingston, New Malden, Surbiton, Tolworth, Hook and Chessington
zones.notes: The Kingston By-Pass (1927, the first purpose-built by-pass in Britain) and Southern electrification (1925-1939) filled the Hogsmill valley. Kingston (-0.3000/51.4120) was an ancient royal borough; Surbiton (-0.3040/51.3920) the railway's own new town of 1838; the 1930s work is Tolworth (-0.2830/51.3780), Hook, Chessington (-0.2990/51.3580, station opened 1939, the line's planned extension to Leatherhead was killed by the Green Belt in 1939 - a good visual beat) and Berrylands. Malden and Coombe UD grew from 12,700 (1921) to 32,000 (1931) to 42,000 (1939). Richmond Park (955 ha, walled 1637) and Bushy Park (445 ha) are the two big permanent voids to the north.
sources: Wikipedia: Kingston upon Thames; Chessington South railway station; Kingston By-Pass

zones.name: Morden, St Helier estate, Merton, Mitcham and Raynes Park
zones.notes: The Northern line was extended from Clapham Common to MORDEN on 13 September 1926 (-0.1950/51.4020) into open fields, and the parish's population rose nine-fold in the ten years to 1931. On the fields immediately east the LCC built the ST HELIER ESTATE 1928-1936 (main construction 1929-34; -0.1900/51.3900), 825 acres straddling the Morden-Carshalton boundary, about 9,068 houses plus 500 flats for around 40,000 people - the SECOND largest LCC cottage estate after Becontree, laid out on garden-city lines with streets named alphabetically after abbeys. St Helier Hospital 1938. Morden Hall Park (National Trust 1941) and Mitcham Common (183 ha) are voids.
sources: Merton Historical Society: St Helier Estate
Layers of London: St Helier Estate 1930
Wikipedia: St Helier, London; Morden tube station

zones.name: The Metropolitan Green Belt - growth stops
zones.notes: CONSTRAINT ZONE, NOT A GROWTH ZONE: this is the OUTER ring; treat the annulus between the 1939 built-up edge and this boundary as permanently forbidden to new growth after about 1947. Sequence: LCC Green Belt scheme 1935 (2 million pounds to buy land); Green Belt (London and Home Counties) Act 1938; Abercrombie's Greater London Plan 1944, which proposed four concentric rings and a 10-mile-wide green belt plus eight new towns beyond it; Town and Country Planning Act 1947, which nationalised development rights and made refusal the default; Ministry Circular 42/55, which invited every authority round London to designate. The result is the single hardest edge in this whole dataset: London's built-up area stops expanding outward after 1939 and from then on all growth is UPWARD or INWARD. The new towns absorbing the overspill - Stevenage 1946, Crawley 1947, Hemel Hempstead 1947, Harlow 1947, Hatfield 1948, Welwyn 1948, Basildon 1949, Bracknell 1949 - are OUTSIDE this frame.
sources: Wikipedia: Metropolitan Green Belt; Greater London Plan; Green Belt (London and Home Counties) Act 1938
Town and Country Planning Act 1947; Circular 42/55

zones.name: Blitz reconstruction and the first wave of council rebuilding
zones.notes: REPLACEMENT OVERLAY on the inner area, not new outward growth. About 1.15 million London houses were damaged and roughly 116,000 destroyed or damaged beyond repair; the County of London alone lost about 3.5 million square metres of floorspace. The response, framed by the County of London Plan 1943 (Forshaw and Abercrombie) and the Greater London Plan 1944, was: prefabs from 1945 (156,000 nationally, 1946-48), then LCC and borough estates on cleared sites, at first 4-5 storey brick blocks and 8-11 storey slabs, from 1955 point blocks - the Housing Subsidy of 1956 paid MORE per flat the higher you built, which is the direct cause of the London tower block. Density here is 0.35 because it patches into an existing fabric. See the 'estates' key for named clusters.
sources: Wikipedia: The Blitz; Council house; County of London Plan 1943
LCC Bomb Damage Maps (London Metropolitan Archives / Layers of London)

zones.name: Out-county overspill estates and the new towns (mostly outside the frame)
