zones.notes: COARSE PLACEHOLDER: the real objects are the discrete out-county estates listed in the 'estates' key - Debden 1947-52, Harold Hill 1948-58, Hainault 1947-53, South Oxhey 1947-52, Borehamwood 1949-55 - each a compact plug of 3,000-8,000 LCC houses dropped beyond the built-up edge in the late 1940s under the Town Development Act 1952 and its predecessors. The eight Mark 1 New Towns designated 1946-49 to take 400,000 Londoners (Stevenage 1946, Crawley, Hemel Hempstead, Harlow, Hatfield, Welwyn 1947-48, Basildon, Bracknell 1949) are all OUTSIDE this frame; mention them in narration but do not model them.
sources: Wikipedia: New Towns Act 1946; Debden; Harold Hill; South Oxhey

zones.name: Outer suburban infill within the Green Belt line, 1950-2025
zones.notes: LOW-PRIORITY OVERLAY at density 0.15: after 1939 the outward edge is frozen, and the only outer growth is infill INSIDE the existing envelope - back-garden development, cul-de-sacs on former nurseries, orchards and playing fields, 1960s-70s private estates on the last farms inside the boundary, flats over suburban shopping parades, and from about 2000 the 'garden grabbing' of large plots for small blocks. Heathrow is the one huge exception and it grows the other way, consuming settlement: the hamlet of Heath Row and Perry Oaks were destroyed for the airport in 1944-46, the terminals opened 1955, Terminal 4 in 1986, Terminal 5 in 2008 on the sludge works (-0.4500/51.4700, 1,227 ha in total).
sources: Wikipedia: Heathrow Airport; Metropolitan Green Belt
GLA London Plan; ONS built-up area statistics

zones.name: Comprehensive redevelopment areas, 1960-1979
zones.notes: REPLACEMENT OVERLAY. Under the 1947 Act's Comprehensive Development Area powers the LCC and then the GLC (1965-86) and the boroughs cleared whole quarters of surviving Victorian terrace - not bombed, just old - and replaced them with system-built slabs, decks and towers. Roughly 384,000 dwellings were demolished in Greater London 1955-1985. Peak years 1965-1972; industrialised systems (Larsen-Nielsen, Bison, Jespersen, Taylor Woodrow-Anglian). The RONAN POINT collapse at Canning Town on 16 May 1968 (0.0170/51.5150, a gas explosion on the 18th floor progressively collapsed one corner of a 22-storey Larsen-Nielsen block, killing 4) ended tower-block housing policy almost overnight: approvals for high flats fell from 26 percent of London's public output in 1966 to near zero by 1975. After it, the kit changes to low-rise, high-density brick - Neave Brown's Alexandra Road (1972-78), Darbourne and Darke's Lillington Gardens (1961-72).
sources: Wikipedia: Ronan Point; Comprehensive development area; Tower block

zones.name: Docklands dereliction - the docks close
zones.notes: NEGATIVE ZONE - remove buildings here between 1967 and 1981. Containerisation killed the upstream docks in fourteen years: East India 1967, St Katharine 1968, London and Surrey Commercial 1969-70, West India and Millwall 1980, Royal Docks 1981 (the last, closing Britain's largest enclosed dock system). About 150,000 dock and dock-related jobs went; the Docklands boroughs lost around 20 percent of their population in the 1970s; roughly 2,200 hectares of derelict land, warehouse and water were left within 8 km of the Bank of England. This is the only large-scale SHRINKAGE in modern London and it makes a very strong beat immediately before the 1980s regeneration.
sources: Wikipedia: London Docklands; Port of London Authority

zones.name: London Docklands regeneration - LDDC, the Enterprise Zone and Canary Wharf
zones.notes: The London Docklands Development Corporation ran 1981-1998 over 2,226 ha with planning powers taken from the boroughs; the Isle of Dogs Enterprise Zone (1982-1992) gave 100 percent capital allowances and no rates. Outputs by 1998: 24,046 new homes, 2.3 million m2 of commercial floorspace, 85,000 jobs, 144 km of new roads, the DLR (opened 31 Aug 1987, extended to Bank 1991, Lewisham 1999), London City Airport (26 Oct 1987) and the Jubilee Line Extension (1999). CANARY WHARF: Olympia and York from 1988, One Canada Square topped out 1990 and occupied Aug 1991 at 235 m and 50 storeys - the tallest building in Britain for 20 years (-0.0235/51.5054). O and Y went bankrupt in May 1992 with the tower two-thirds empty; recovery from 1995, HSBC and Citigroup towers (both 200 m) in 2001-02. Also: Surrey Quays 1984-95 and its shopping centre 1988; Wapping warehouse conversions and News International's move in 1986; Beckton and Royal Docks housing; ExCeL 2000.
sources: Wikipedia: London Docklands Development Corporation; Canary Wharf; One Canada Square

zones.name: Inner-London brownfield densification, 1990-2025
zones.notes: REPLACEMENT OVERLAY: after PPG3 (2000) and the first London Plan (2004) set a brownfield-first, high-density policy, London's growth turned entirely inward. Greater London's population, which had fallen from 8.6 million in 1939 to 6.61 million in 1988, climbed back to 8.17 million in 2011 and 8.8 million in 2021 with almost NO increase in built-up area (1,738 km2 at the 2011 census). Growth appears as: gasworks, goods yards, hospitals, breweries and industrial estates replaced by 6-12 storey blocks; former council estates rebuilt at higher density; and the tall-building clusters in the 'towers' key. The Elephant and Castle (Heygate demolished 2011-14, Elephant Park 2013-2025), King's Cross Central (27 ha, 2007-2022), White City (Westfield 2008, Television Centre 2015-18), Nine Elms, Wembley Park and Canada Water are the biggest single sites.
sources: Wikipedia: Greater London Built-up Area; London Plan

zones.name: Greenwich Peninsula and the Millennium Dome
zones.notes: 121 ha of the most contaminated land in Britain - the East Greenwich Gasworks (1886-1985) was the largest in Europe. Remediated 1997-98; the Millennium Dome (Richard Rogers, 365 m diameter, 12 masts of 100 m) built 1997-1999, opened 31 Dec 1999, reopened as The O2 in 2007 (0.0030/51.5030); Greenwich Millennium Village from 1999 (Ralph Erskine); North Greenwich Jubilee line station 1999; the Emirates Air Line cable car 2012 (closed as such 2024). The wider peninsula masterplan is for 15,700-17,700 homes to the 2030s, so this zone is still growing at the end of the timelapse.
sources: Wikipedia: Greenwich Peninsula; Millennium Dome; The O2

zones.name: Thames Gateway east - Barking Riverside, Beckton and Rainham
zones.notes: The last big greenfield-scale growth inside Greater London, on the old Barking Power Station ash fields and Thames marshes. Barking Riverside: 179 ha, outline consent 2007, 10,800 homes planned, first phase 2013, the London Overground extension and new station opened 18 July 2022 (0.1230/51.5190). Beckton, Gallions Reach and the Royal Docks Enterprise Zone (2012) alongside. Everything here is post-2000 and much of it is post-2015 - it is the only place on the map still going green-to-grey in the final seconds of the timelapse.
sources: Wikipedia: Barking Riverside; Thames Gateway; Royal Docks

zones.name: Stratford City, the Olympic Park and East Village
zones.notes: London won the 2012 Games on 6 July 2005; 246 ha of contaminated railway land, scrapyards and the Lea navigation at Stratford Marsh were compulsorily purchased, 200,000 m3 of soil washed, and the park built 2008-2011. Stadium 2008-11 (-0.0166/51.5386, 80,000 seats, reduced to 62,500 for West Ham 2016); Aquatics Centre (Zaha Hadid) 2008-11; Velodrome 2011; the ArcelorMittal Orbit 2012 (114.5 m). Westfield Stratford City, then Europe's largest urban shopping centre, opened 13 Sep 2011 (-0.0055/51.5435). The Athletes' Village became EAST VILLAGE, 2,818 homes handed over 2013 (-0.0110/51.5450). Legacy phases - Chobham Manor 2015, East Wick and Sweetwater 2018-2030, East Bank (V and A East, Sadler's Wells, BBC, UCL East) 2022-2026 - carry the zone to about 2030.
sources: Wikipedia: Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park; East Village, London; Westfield Stratford City

estates.name: Boundary Estate, Shoreditch
estates.notes: The first council housing estate in the world, built by the LCC on the cleared Old Nichol rookery. 5,719 people were displaced and only 11 of them were rehoused. Red-brick blocks radiating from the raised Arnold Circus bandstand, which is built on the rubble of the slum.
sources: LCC Housing of the Working Classes 1855-1912

estates.name: Millbank Estate, Westminster
estates.notes: LCC, built with bricks from the demolished Millbank Penitentiary; blocks named after English painters.

estates.name: Totterdown Fields, Tooting
estates.notes: The FIRST LCC out-county cottage estate - two-storey terraces at 30 to the acre, reached by the new LCC electric tram. Direct ancestor of Becontree.

estates.name: Tower Gardens / White Hart Lane, Tottenham
estates.notes: LCC cottage estate in Arts and Crafts style, part-funded by Samuel Montagu to rehouse Jewish East Enders.

estates.name: Old Oak Estate, East Acton
estates.notes: LCC cottage estate; the earliest phase 1911-13 is the purest Parker-and-Unwin garden-suburb work the LCC ever did.

estates.name: Progress Estate / Well Hall, Eltham
estates.notes: Built by HM Office of Works in 10 months in 1915 for Woolwich Arsenal munitions workers, architect Frank Baines. 1,298 houses and flats in Arts and Crafts style on curving lanes; the template for the entire 1919 'Homes fit for Heroes' programme.

estates.name: Dover House Estate, Roehampton
estates.notes: LCC cottage estate on the Dover House and Putney Park estates - the most consciously garden-suburb of all the LCC estates, and the reason the Alton Estate later went up next door.

estates.name: Bellingham Estate, Catford
estates.notes: LCC cottage estate on the Bellingham Farm land bought in 1919; laid out around a central green.

estates.name: Downham Estate, Bromley/Lewisham
estates.notes: LCC cottage estate for 30,000 people, named after the LCC chairman Lord Downham. Famous for the 'Downham Wall' - a 2 m brick wall built across Alexandra Crescent in 1926 by the private residents of Bromley to keep the council tenants out; it stood until 1950.

estates.name: Castelnau Estate, Barnes
estates.notes: LCC cottage estate on the Thames loop at Barnes.

estates.name: Watling Estate, Burnt Oak
estates.notes: LCC cottage estate for about 19,000 people beside the new Burnt Oak tube station (1924), astride Watling Street. Ruth Durant's 'Watling: A Survey of Social Life on a New Housing Estate' (1939) is the classic sociology of interwar council suburbia.

estates.name: White City Estate, Hammersmith
estates.notes: LCC flatted estate on the site of the 1908 Franco-British Exhibition and Olympic stadium; five-storey brick blocks, the mature interwar LCC flat kit. Largely rebuilt from 2015.

estates.name: Churchill Gardens, Pimlico
estates.notes: Won in open competition in 1946 by Powell and Moya, then aged 24 and 25 - the first major postwar council scheme, 13.5 ha of bombed Pimlico. Heated by waste hot water piped under the Thames from Battersea Power Station via the surviving glass 'Accumulator Tower'.

estates.name: Woodberry Down, Manor House
estates.notes: Planned from 1938 and built 1946-62 as the LCC's showpiece 'estate of the future' beside the New River reservoirs, with Britain's first purpose-built comprehensive school (1955) and first health centre (1952). Under total rebuild since 2009 - about 5,500 homes by the 2030s.

estates.name: Spa Green Estate, Finsbury
estates.notes: Berthold Lubetkin and Tecton for Finsbury Borough - designed 1938, built 1946-50; the first serious Modernist council housing in Britain, with Ove Arup's box-frame structure and an aerofoil roof for drying laundry. Grade II* listed.

estates.name: Excalibur prefab estate, Catford
estates.notes: 186 Uni-Seco single-storey prefabs put up by German and Italian POWs in 1946 as temporary housing for 10 years; most survived to 2013. Stands for the 156,000 prefabs erected nationally 1945-48 - Britain's fastest ever housing programme.

estates.name: Priory Green Estate, Islington
estates.notes: Lubetkin and Skinner for Finsbury; the second of the Finsbury Plan estates.

estates.name: Debden estate, Loughton (LCC out-county)
estates.notes: LCC out-county estate of about 4,000 houses beyond the Green Belt on the Central line extension (Debden station 1949) - the classic 'East End goes to Essex' migration. Population about 15,000 by 1955.

estates.name: Hainault estate, Redbridge (LCC out-county)
estates.notes: LCC out-county estate on the former Hainault Forest farmland, served by the Central line extension of 1948.

estates.name: South Oxhey, Watford (LCC out-county)
estates.notes: About 4,000 LCC houses on the Oxhey Place estate in Hertfordshire, built 1947-52 for around 14,000 Londoners; its own station (Carpenders Park moved 1952). Just outside the Greater London boundary but well inside the visual frame.

estates.name: Harold Hill estate, Romford (LCC out-county)
estates.notes: The largest LCC out-county estate - about 7,600 dwellings for 25,000 people on 500 ha of Essex farmland, built 1948-58 with its own neighbourhood centres, schools and an industrial estate at Harold Wood.

estates.name: Borehamwood LCC estates
estates.notes: About 3,000 LCC houses in Hertfordshire under the 1952 Town Development Act model; the town's population trebled in six years.

estates.name: Lansbury Estate, Poplar
estates.notes: The Festival of Britain's 'Live Architecture Exhibition' of 1951 - a working neighbourhood built on blitzed Poplar as a public demonstration of the new planning: mixed development, a pedestrian market square, Chrisp Street Market clock tower (Frederick Gibberd), church, school and pub.

estates.name: South Acton Estate
estates.notes: The largest estate in west London, built in successive waves from 1949 to the late 1970s - cottages, then slabs, then Bison towers. Under rebuild as 'Acton Gardens' (about 3,400 homes) since 2010.
sources: Wikipedia: South Acton, London; Acton Gardens

estates.name: Alton East, Roehampton
estates.notes: LCC Architect's Department, the 'Swedish' humanist wing - 11-storey point blocks and low terraces set among the mature trees of the old Roehampton villa grounds.
sources: Layers of London: Alton East Estate

estates.name: Golden Lane Estate, City of London
estates.notes: Chamberlin, Powell and Bon won the City's 1952 competition; Great Arthur House (1957, 16 storeys) was briefly the tallest residential block in Britain. Its success got the same architects the Barbican commission.

estates.name: Golden Lane and Barbican combined City rebuild
estates.notes: Convenience record for the whole Cripplegate rebuild - see e26 and e33. The City's resident population had fallen to 5,324 by 1951 and the Corporation deliberately built these estates to bring residents back; it is now about 8,600.

estates.name: Loughborough Estate, Brixton
estates.notes: LCC mixed development - nine 11-storey slab blocks with maisonettes and terraces between; the LCC Architect's Department's first big statement of the Corbusian slab in south London.

estates.name: Alton West, Roehampton
estates.notes: The Corbusian wing of the same LCC office - five 12-storey slab blocks on pilotis, directly modelled on the Unite d'Habitation, striding down the slope above Richmond Park. The most internationally famous public housing in Britain and the setting of Truffaut's Fahrenheit 451 (1966).

estates.name: Cranbrook Estate, Bethnal Green
estates.notes: Lubetkin's last work, with Skinner and Bailey, for Bethnal Green: six towers of 8-15 storeys on a diagonal Beaux-Arts plan with a Karel Vogel sculpture on the axis.

estates.name: Keeling House, Bethnal Green
estates.notes: Denys Lasdun's 'cluster block' - four maisonette towers around a service core, an attempt to reproduce the East End street in the air. Grade II* listed in 1993, the first postwar council block to be listed; sold and refurbished privately in 1999.

estates.name: Brandon Estate, Kennington
estates.notes: The LCC's first estate to combine 18-storey point blocks with refurbished Georgian terraces rather than sweeping them away, and the first to buy public art for a housing estate (Henry Moore's 'Two-Piece Reclining Figure No. 3', 1961).

estates.name: Lillington Gardens, Pimlico
estates.notes: Darbourne and Darke won the 1961 competition; red brick, stepped, dense and low - the earliest and most influential London rejection of the concrete slab, and the source of the 1970s brick-and-planting housing kit used all over the city.
sources: Wikipedia: Lillington and Longmoore Gardens Estate

estates.name: Warwick and Brindley Estates, Westbourne Green
estates.notes: Paddington/Westminster towers and slabs on the Grand Union Canal, replacing the Rachman-era slum lettings of Westbourne Park.

estates.name: Aylesbury Estate, Walworth
estates.notes: Southwark Council, 2,704 dwellings for about 10,000 people on 24 ha - one of the largest estates in Europe, built in Jespersen large-panel system with elevated walkways linking every block. Tony Blair's first speech as Prime Minister was made here on 2 June 1997. Demolition and rebuild began 2010 and is still running.

estates.name: Winstanley and York Road Estates, Battersea
estates.notes: Battersea/Wandsworth towers and slabs beside Clapham Junction; under rebuild since 2021 (about 2,550 homes).

estates.name: Balfron Tower, Poplar
estates.notes: Erno Goldfinger, GLC - 26 storeys, 84 m, with the lifts and services in a detached tower linked by walkways every three floors. Goldfinger and his wife lived in flat 130 for two months in 1968 to test it. Grade II* listed; refurbished for private sale 2015-2022.

estates.name: Barbican Estate, City of London
estates.notes: Chamberlin, Powell and Bon on 14 ha of the most completely destroyed part of the City (the night of 29 Dec 1940 left almost nothing standing from Moorgate to Aldersgate). 2,014 flats, three 42-43 storey towers of 123 m - the tallest residential buildings in Europe when finished - all in bush-hammered concrete, over a network of raised walkways and lakes; the Barbican Centre followed in 1982. Grade II listed 2001.

estates.name: Chalkhill Estate, Wembley
estates.notes: Wembley/Brent Council, 1,857 dwellings in Bison large-panel system with a kilometre of elevated deck. Demolished 1997-2003 and replaced with 1,500 low-rise houses.

estates.name: North Peckham Estate
estates.notes: Southwark's deck-access estate - 65 five-storey blocks linked by walkways over 16 ha. Demolished 1998-2006 under the Peckham Partnership after the murder of Damilola Taylor there in 2000; replaced by the Peckham Park low-rise streets.

estates.name: Pepys Estate, Deptford
estates.notes: GLC, on the 18 ha Royal Victoria Victualling Yard which closed in 1961 - three 24-storey towers and deck-access slabs with a river frontage. Aragon Tower was sold to Berkeley Homes in 2002, the first sale of a whole council tower for private conversion.

estates.name: Ronan Point, Canning Town
estates.notes: THE pivotal event of postwar London housing. A 22-storey Larsen-Nielsen block completed in March 1968; at 05:45 on 16 May 1968 a gas explosion in flat 90 blew out a load-bearing wall panel and the whole south-east corner progressively collapsed, killing 4 and injuring 17. It ended system-built high-rise housing in Britain: the Fifth Amendment to the Building Regulations (1970) required disproportionate-collapse resistance, and high-flat approvals collapsed to near zero by 1975. Ronan Point itself was demolished in 1986.

estates.name: Holly Street Estate, Dalston
estates.notes: Hackney - four 19-storey towers and serpentine deck-access 'snake blocks'. Demolished 1993-2003 and rebuilt as low-rise streets; the pioneering London example of comprehensive estate replacement.

estates.name: Thamesmead
estates.notes: The GLC's own new town on 526 ha of Erith and Plumstead marshes and the former Royal Arsenal ranges - first pile driven 1967, first tenants 1968, planned for 60,000 people but only about 11,000 dwellings were ever built. Raised concrete decks and elevated walkways above the flood level, linked lakes and canals. Kubrick filmed A Clockwork Orange (1971) at Southmere. No railway station was ever built (the Crossrail/DLR extension is still unbuilt in 2025), which is the standard explanation for its isolation. Under a 30-year rebuild by Peabody since 2014.
sources: GLC Department of Architecture and Civic Design

estates.name: Broadwater Farm, Tottenham
estates.notes: Haringey, 12 blocks in Largo panel system raised on stilts above the Moselle brook flood plain, with ground level given over to garages and walkways. Site of the riot of 6 October 1985 in which PC Keith Blakelock was killed; the walkways were removed and the ground floors reoccupied from 1986 in one of the first big estate 'defensible space' retrofits.

estates.name: Stonebridge Estate, Harlesden
estates.notes: Brent Council, deck-access blocks and towers; by the 1990s among the most deprived wards in England. Demolished and rebuilt 1997-2010 by the Stonebridge Housing Action Trust.

estates.name: Doddington and Rollo Estate, Battersea
estates.notes: GLC, towers and long slabs on cleared Victorian Battersea.

estates.name: Ferrier Estate, Kidbrooke
estates.notes: GLC, 1,906 dwellings in Larsen-Nielsen large panels on the former RAF Kidbrooke site. Demolished 2009-2012 and replaced by Kidbrooke Village (about 4,800 homes, Berkeley, 2010-2030s).

estates.name: Nightingale Estate, Hackney
estates.notes: Hackney/GLC, six 22-storey Bison towers on Hackney Downs. Five towers demolished 1998-2003 and replaced by low-rise; one, Seaton Point, retained.

estates.name: Robin Hood Gardens, Poplar
estates.notes: Alison and Peter Smithson's 'streets in the sky' - two long curved slabs of 7 and 10 storeys facing each other across an artificial mound, buffered from the Blackwall Tunnel approach by concrete fins. Refused listing three times and demolished 2017-2025; one three-storey section is in the V and A collection.

estates.name: Dawson's Heights, East Dulwich
estates.notes: Designed by Kate Macintosh at 26 for Southwark - two stepped ziggurat blocks on a hilltop, one of the very few 1960s London estates that has never been unpopular.

estates.name: Trellick Tower, North Kensington
estates.notes: Erno Goldfinger's GLC masterpiece and the taller sibling of Balfron: 31 storeys, 98 m, detached service tower with boiler house on top. Notorious in the 1970s-80s, Grade II* listed in 1998, and now one of the most desirable addresses in west London.

estates.name: Ledbury Estate, Peckham
estates.notes: Four 14-storey Large Panel System towers by Southwark - directly comparable to Ronan Point, and evacuated in 2017 when post-Grenfell surveys found the same structural weaknesses; demolition agreed 2021.

estates.name: World's End Estate, Chelsea
estates.notes: Eric Lyons, Cadbury-Brown, Metcalfe and Cunningham for Kensington and Chelsea - seven interlinked polygonal brick towers of up to 21 storeys on the river at the far end of the King's Road; deliberately red brick rather than concrete, an early reaction against the slab.

estates.name: Lancaster West Estate and Grenfell Tower, North Kensington
estates.notes: Kensington and Chelsea; Grenfell Tower (-0.2163/51.5139) was completed in 1974 at 24 storeys and 67.3 m. Overclad in 2015-16 with polyethylene-cored ACM panels; the fire of 14 June 2017 killed 72 people, the worst residential fire in Britain since 1666, and led to the Building Safety Act 2022 and the national cladding remediation programme. The tower is due to be taken down to ground level from 2025-26.
sources: Wikipedia: Grenfell Tower fire; Lancaster West Estate

estates.name: Heygate Estate, Elephant and Castle
estates.notes: Southwark, Tim Tinker, completed 1974 - 1,214 dwellings in long slabs round a green. Decanted from 2007, demolished 2011-2014 and replaced by Elephant Park (about 3,000 homes, of which 82 are social rent), the most contested estate regeneration in London.

estates.name: Alexandra Road (Rowley Way), Camden
estates.notes: Neave Brown for Camden - two long stepped terraces of in-situ white concrete along a pedestrian street, curved to shield the flats from the West Coast Main Line. Low-rise, high-density (about 210 habitable rooms per hectare, denser than the towers it replaced) - the definitive answer to the tower block. Grade II* listed in 1993, the first postwar housing estate to be listed.

estates.name: Andover Estate, Finsbury Park
estates.notes: Islington Borough, deck-access brick blocks of the post-Ronan-Point generation; partially remodelled from 1997.

estates.name: Angell Town Estate, Brixton
estates.notes: Lambeth deck-access estate; remodelled from 1994 in one of the earliest tenant-led regeneration schemes in Britain.

estates.name: Kidbrooke Village (Ferrier replacement)
estates.notes: Berkeley Homes' replacement of the Ferrier Estate - about 4,800 homes on 34 ha, 2010 to the 2030s. Included here as the standard template for post-2000 estate regeneration: demolish 1,900 council flats, build 4,800 mostly private homes.

towers.name: Croydon
towers.notes: London's only true outer-borough high-rise centre, and it happened twice. First wave: the Croydon Corporation Act 1956 let the borough build offices without London-wide controls, and 1962-1970 produced about 500,000 m2 of office towers - St George's House 1964, 82 m; the NLA Tower ('the Threepenny Bit Building') 1970, 82 m (-0.0940/51.3730). Second wave, residential: Saffron Square 2015, 134 m; Ten Degrees / College Road 2020, two towers of 135 m and 120 m - at the time the tallest modular buildings in the world (-0.0973/51.3742).
sources: Wikipedia: Croydon; NLA Tower; Ten Degrees
Croydon Council Vision 2020 / Croydon Opportunity Area

towers.name: The City cluster (Bishopsgate / Leadenhall / Undershaft)
towers.notes: The only tall cluster in the historic core, deliberately confined by the St Paul's protected view corridors (the London View Management Framework, 13 protected vistas) and the City's own 'Eastern Cluster' policy. Sequence: Tower 42 / NatWest Tower 1980, 183 m (-0.0817/51.5152); 30 St Mary Axe, the Gherkin, 2001-04, 180 m (-0.0803/51.5145); Broadgate Tower 2008, 164 m; Heron Tower 2011, 230 m with mast (-0.0817/51.5170); The Leadenhall Building, the Cheesegrater, 2014, 225 m (-0.0821/51.5138); 20 Fenchurch Street, the Walkie-Talkie, 2014, 160 m (-0.0836/51.5114); 22 Bishopsgate 2020, 278 m and 62 storeys, the tallest in the City (-0.0813/51.5152); 8 Bishopsgate 2023, 204 m. 1 Undershaft, 309.6 m, consented 2024 and due about 2030-32, would equal the Shard. Nearly all offices, not homes.
sources: Wikipedia: List of tallest buildings in London; 22 Bishopsgate
City of London Corporation tall buildings policy

towers.name: Canary Wharf and the Isle of Dogs
towers.notes: Britain's second business district, on the West India Docks. One Canada Square 1988-91, 235 m, 50 storeys, Cesar Pelli - the tallest building in Britain 1991-2010 (-0.0235/51.5054); 8 Canada Square (HSBC) and 25 Canada Square (Citigroup), both 200 m, 2001-02; then a residential second wave - Landmark Pinnacle 2020, 233 m, 75 storeys (-0.0192/51.5010); Newfoundland 2020, 220 m; South Quay Plaza 2020, 215 m; Wardian, Baltimore Tower. From an office park of 40 towers to a residential district of about 3,500 homes built 2015-2025 and 10,000 more planned. The Isle of Dogs went from 0 to roughly 40 buildings above 100 m in 35 years - the sharpest skyline change anywhere in Britain.
sources: Wikipedia: Canary Wharf; One Canada Square

towers.name: Paddington Basin and Paddington Square
towers.notes: 11 ha of canal basin and goods yard beside Brunel's station. Waterside (Marks and Spencer HQ) 2004; the Point 2003; Merchant Square 2010-2020 including One Merchant Square, 42 storeys; Paddington Square 2022 by Renzo Piano, a 19-storey glass cube over a new Bakerloo entrance (-0.1750/51.5158). The Elizabeth line opened here 24 May 2022.

towers.name: Woolwich and Royal Arsenal Riverside
towers.notes: Berkeley's 30 ha Royal Arsenal Riverside (about 5,000 homes, 2000-2030s) on the Arsenal that closed in 1994, plus the Woolwich town-centre towers. The Elizabeth line station opened 24 May 2022 and the DLR arrived in 2009 - the transport that made 20-storey towers viable this far east.

towers.name: Colindale and Hendon
towers.notes: The one place where OUTER London densifies hard: Beaufort Park on the former RAF Hendon aerodrome and Hendon Police College land, 2007-2016, about 2,900 homes; Colindale Gardens on the old National Institute for Medical Research site, 2016-2028, about 2,900 homes; Grahame Park estate (1971) under rebuild. 12-20 storey blocks in what was a 1930s semi-detached suburb.
sources: Barnet Council Colindale Area Action Plan

towers.name: Elephant and Castle
towers.notes: Strata SE1, 2010, 148 m, 43 storeys with three wind turbines in its crown (-0.0985/51.4936); One The Elephant 2016, 122 m; Elephant Park (Lendlease, on the demolished Heygate) 2013-2025, about 3,000 homes; the 1965 shopping centre demolished 2021 and replaced 2023-2026. The area also carries Southwark's 1960s towers, so it reads as two generations of high-rise on the same ground.
sources: Wikipedia: Elephant and Castle; Strata SE1

towers.name: White City and Old Oak
towers.notes: Westfield London opened 30 October 2008 (-0.2210/51.5070), then White City Place on the BBC land - Television Centre (1960, Grade II listed 2009) converted 2015-18 - and White City Living (St James, 2017-2028, about 2,500 homes). Beyond it Old Oak Common (-0.2500/51.5320) is the largest regeneration site in Britain: the HS2 and Elizabeth line interchange under construction since 2019 with an eventual 25,500 homes to the 2040s, but almost nothing built by 2025 - so at the end of the timelapse it should still read as railway land.
sources: Wikipedia: White City, London; Old Oak Common

towers.name: King's Cross Central
towers.notes: NOT a tower cluster - include it here for completeness but build it at 6-12 storeys. 27 ha of railway lands behind King's Cross and St Pancras, outline consent 2006, built 2008-2022: 2,000 homes, 50 new or restored buildings, 10 new public squares, Central Saint Martins in the 1851 Granary (2011), Coal Drops Yard (Heatherwick, 2018), Google's 'landscraper' HQ (330 m long, 11 storeys, 2024-25), Gasholders London (2018, inside three restored 1860s gasholder frames, -0.1265/51.5372). The best-regarded large regeneration in modern London and a good visual counterpoint to Nine Elms.
sources: Wikipedia: King's Cross Central; Coal Drops Yard

towers.name: The Shard and London Bridge Quarter
towers.notes: Renzo Piano's Shard, built 2009-2012 on the site of Southwark Towers over London Bridge station: 309.6 m, 72 habitable storeys, the tallest building in the United Kingdom and (briefly) in the European Union. Its planning consent in 2003, after a public inquiry, is the moment London policy formally accepted very tall buildings outside the City. News Building (The Place) 2010, 100 m; Guy's Tower 1974, 148 m, next door.

towers.name: Vauxhall, Nine Elms and Battersea
towers.notes: The Vauxhall Nine Elms Battersea Opportunity Area - 195 ha of railway land, the New Covent Garden Market and Battersea Power Station, for about 20,000 homes and 25,000 jobs, the largest regeneration zone in central London. St George Wharf Tower 2014, 181 m, 50 storeys, London's tallest wholly residential building at the time (-0.1245/51.4864); Damac Tower 2020, 50 storeys; One Nine Elms 2023, 200 m (-0.1281/51.4834); Embassy Gardens and the US Embassy, opened January 2018 (-0.1301/51.4837); Battersea Power Station (Giles Gilbert Scott 1929-55, derelict 1983-2013) redeveloped 2013-2022 and reopened to the public on 14 October 2022 (-0.1440/51.4816), with Frank Gehry's Prospect Place alongside. The Northern line extension to Nine Elms and Battersea Power Station opened 20 September 2021 - the first Tube extension of the 21st century.
sources: Wikipedia: Nine Elms; Battersea Power Station; St George Wharf Tower
GLA VNEB Opportunity Area Planning Framework 2012

towers.name: Lewisham town centre
towers.notes: Lewisham Gateway 2014-2023 (about 1,000 homes on the rerouted Ravensbourne confluence) and the Renaissance towers 2011-2015 (up to 24 storeys) - an outer-inner borough centre going high-rise on the strength of the DLR extension of 1999 and 15-minute journeys to Canary Wharf.

towers.name: South Bank and Blackfriars Road
towers.notes: South Bank Tower (the 1972 King's Reach Tower re-clad and extended to 41 storeys, 2016, 152 m); One Blackfriars, 'the Vase', 2018, 163 m (-0.1050/51.5075); the Southbank Place towers on the old Shell Centre site, 2019 (-0.1180/51.5035). Runs along the tourist riverfront and is therefore the most photographed new skyline in London after the City.
sources: Wikipedia: One Blackfriars; South Bank Tower

towers.name: Stratford and the Olympic fringe
towers.notes: Manhattan Loft Gardens 2019, 143 m, 42 storeys with three sky gardens (-0.0035/51.5418); Stratford Halo 2013, 132 m; Legacy Wharf, Sugar House Island, Stratford Cross. Newham has consented more tall buildings since 2010 than any other London borough. The area also holds the ArcelorMittal Orbit 2012, 114.5 m, Britain's largest sculpture (-0.0129/51.5386).
sources: Wikipedia: Manhattan Loft Gardens; Stratford, London

towers.name: Wembley Park
towers.notes: Quintain's 34 ha scheme around the new Wembley Stadium (2003-2007, 90,000 seats, 133 m arch replacing the 1923 Twin Towers demolished in 2003) - about 8,500 homes, mostly build-to-rent, in 15-26 storey blocks, built 2013-2027. The London Designer Outlet 2013 and the SSE/OVO Arena (the 1934 Empire Pool) sit inside it.

towers.name: Blackwall, Poplar Riverside and Leamouth
towers.notes: City Island at Leamouth (2016-2020, about 1,700 homes on the Bow Creek peninsula, -0.0075/51.5090), Poplar Riverside (2021-2035, about 2,800 homes), Aberfeldy Village. The overspill of the Canary Wharf cluster eastwards along the Lea mouth.

towers.name: Southall Green Quarter and west London densification
towers.notes: The Green Quarter at Southall - 3,750 homes on the former Southall Gas Works, 2016-2035 - plus Ealing's town-centre towers (Dickens Yard 2015, Filmworks 2021). Included to show that post-2015 tall-building growth is no longer confined to the centre and the east.
sources: Ealing Council Local Plan; Berkeley Group

towers.name: Canada Water and Surrey Quays
towers.notes: British Land's 21 ha masterplan on the Surrey Commercial Docks and the 1988 shopping centre - outline consent 2020, about 3,000 homes and a new town centre to the mid-2030s, with towers up to 34 storeys. The first buildings completed 2024-25, so this is one of the very last things to appear in the timelapse.

voids.name: Hyde Park and Kensington Gardens
voids.notes: Seized from Westminster Abbey by Henry VIII in 1536 as a hunting park; opened to the public by Charles I in 1637. Kensington Gardens split off 1728. Never built on.

voids.name: St James's Park
voids.notes: Drained and enclosed by Henry VIII 1532; relandscaped by Nash 1826-27. The oldest Royal Park.

voids.name: Green Park
voids.notes: Enclosed by Charles II 1668.

voids.name: Regent's Park and Primrose Hill
voids.notes: Crown land (Marylebone Park); Nash scheme 1811, opened to the public 1835. London Zoo 1828 inside its northern edge.

voids.name: Hampstead Heath and Kenwood
voids.notes: Saved by the Hampstead Heath Act 1871 after a 40-year fight with the lord of the manor; extended by Parliament Hill 1888, Golders Hill 1898, Kenwood 1928. The single most consequential open-space campaign in London and the reason north-west London has a hole in it.

voids.name: Richmond Park
voids.notes: Walled by Charles I in 1637; the largest enclosed space in London, larger than the whole medieval city many times over.

voids.name: Bushy Park and Hampton Court Home Park
voids.notes: Henry VIII took Hampton Court from Wolsey in 1529; Bushy Park's Chestnut Avenue laid out by Wren 1699.

voids.name: Wimbledon Common and Putney Heath
voids.notes: Saved by the Wimbledon and Putney Commons Act 1871 after Earl Spencer tried to enclose and build.

voids.name: Clapham Common
voids.notes: Metropolitan Commons Act; the Victorian terraces stop dead at its edge.

voids.name: Tooting Bec and Tooting Graveney Commons
Epping Forest (southern end, in frame)
voids.notes: Epping Forest Act 1878, bought and defended by the City of London Corporation, dedicated by Queen Victoria in 1882 'for the enjoyment of my people for ever'. It is the hardest north-eastern edge in the model - Walthamstow and Chingford stop against it in 1935 and have never crossed it.

voids.name: Wanstead Flats and Wanstead Park
voids.notes: Part of Epping Forest; the reason there is a green wedge between Leyton and Ilford.

voids.name: Hainault Forest and Fairlop Plain
voids.notes: Most of Hainault Forest was grubbed up in 1851; the remnant was bought for the public in 1903-06.

voids.name: Victoria Park, Hackney
voids.notes: The first purpose-built public park in London, opened 1845 after a 30,000-signature East End petition; a deliberate public-health response to the 1832 cholera epidemic.

voids.name: Hackney Marshes and Lee Valley south
voids.notes: Bought by the LCC in 1893. With the Lee Valley Regional Park (1967) it forms a continuous green corridor 42 km long that has kept the Lea valley from being built on.

voids.name: Walthamstow and Chingford reservoirs, Lee Valley
voids.notes: East London Waterworks reservoirs from 1863, King George V 1913, William Girling 1951. Water, not park, but equally unbuildable - and the reason Tottenham and Walthamstow never merged.

voids.name: Greenwich Park
voids.notes: Enclosed 1433, the oldest enclosed Royal Park; the Royal Observatory (1675) sits on its hill and defines longitude 0.

voids.name: Blackheath
voids.notes: Common land; the Victorian terraces of Blackheath and Lee ring it precisely.

voids.name: Woolwich Common, Oxleas Wood and Shooters Hill
voids.notes: Military common plus ancient woodland; the 1993 defeat of the East London River Crossing road scheme saved Oxleas Wood.

voids.name: Dulwich - park, woods, golf course and playing fields
voids.notes: Edward Alleyn's 1619 endowment left the Dulwich College estate holding the freehold of 600 ha; it refused to sell and let only on tight covenants, which is why there is a low-density green hole in the middle of dense south London.

voids.name: Crystal Palace Park
voids.notes: Laid out 1852-54 for the re-erected Crystal Palace, which burned down on 30 November 1936; the terraces, sphinxes and the 1854 dinosaurs survive.

voids.name: Battersea Park
voids.notes: Made out of Battersea Fields 1854-58 with spoil from the Victoria Dock excavation; Festival Pleasure Gardens 1951.

voids.name: Wormwood Scrubs
voids.notes: Protected by its own Act of Parliament in 1879; the prison of 1874-91 sits on its edge.

voids.name: Kensal Green Cemetery
voids.notes: The first of the 'Magnificent Seven' commercial cemeteries created after the 1832 Burial Act - the others (Highgate 1839, Nunhead 1840, Brompton 1840, Abney Park 1840, West Norwood 1837, Tower Hamlets 1841) are all permanent voids inside the Victorian fabric.

voids.name: Alexandra Park
voids.notes: Alexandra Palace 1873 (burned and rebuilt within two years); the BBC made the world's first regular high-definition television broadcasts from here on 2 November 1936.

voids.name: Finsbury Park
voids.notes: One of the first parks created by the Metropolitan Board of Works.

voids.name: Kew Gardens, Old Deer Park and Syon Park
voids.notes: Royal Botanic Gardens from 1759, a World Heritage Site since 2003; Syon Park opposite has been Percy land since 1594.

voids.name: Osterley Park
voids.notes: Given to the National Trust in 1949; a large green hole inside the interwar Middlesex suburb.

voids.name: Trent Park and the Enfield Chase remnant
voids.notes: Opened as a country park in 1973; part of the Green Belt line that stops Cockfosters and Southgate growing north.

voids.name: Hounslow Heath, the Crane valley and the west London reservoirs
voids.notes: Heath remnant plus the Queen Mary (1925) and King George VI (1947) reservoirs - unbuildable and the reason the interwar suburb stops where it does south-west of Hounslow.

voids.name: Heathrow Airport
voids.notes: NOT green, but a permanent hole in the residential fabric AND a rare case of London destroying settlement: the hamlet of Heath Row, Perry Oaks and Cain's Lane were demolished for the airfield in 1944-46. Civil airport 1946, terminals from 1955, Terminal 4 in 1986, Terminal 5 in 2008. The public safety zones and noise contours have suppressed housing over a much wider area than the airport itself.

voids.name: The River Thames and the tidal creeks
voids.notes: LINEAR VOID - trace the modern channel. Remember the historic river was much WIDER and shallower: the Roman and medieval north bank at the City ran roughly along Thames Street, 100-150 m north of the modern wall; the Victoria Embankment (1864-70, Bazalgette) reclaimed about 15 ha between Westminster and Blackfriars; the Albert (1866-69) and Chelsea (1871-74) Embankments did the same on the south and west. Before 1700 the Isle of Dogs, Bermondsey, Lambeth, Rotherhithe, Plaistow and Erith were tidal marsh behind walls, and the Lea, Ravensbourne, Wandle, Fleet, Walbrook, Tyburn, Westbourne, Effra and Neckinger were open streams.
